會試錄序

皇上御極之三十八年春，復當會試天下士。士集禮部待試者四千六百人有竒，尚書臣吳山、侍郎臣茅瓚、臣袁煒以聞。於是，上命學士臣李璣、臣嚴訥往典試事。其同考試，則侍讀臣胡正蒙、臣姜金和，修撰臣林燫、臣諸大綬，編修臣曹大章、臣李貴、臣王希烈、臣趙祖鵬，檢討臣晁瑮、臣馬自強、臣馬一龍，都給事中臣趙鏘、臣藍璧、臣王文炳，郎中臣王秩，員外郎
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the spring of the thirty-eighth year since His Majesty ascended the throne, it was once again time to hold the Metropolitan Examination for the scholars of the realm. More than 4,600 scholars assembled at the Ministry of Rites awaiting examination. Your servants Wu Shan, Minister, and Mao Zan and Yuan Wei, Vice Ministers, reported this to the throne. His Majesty thereupon ordered your servants Li Ji and Yan Na, Academicians, to take charge of the examination.

The Associate Examiners were your servants Hu Zhengmeng and Jiang Jinhe, Readers-in-Waiting; Lin Lian and Zhu Dashou, Senior Compilers; Cao Dazhang, Li Gui, Wang Xilie, and Zhao Zupeng, Junior Compilers; Chao Li, Ma Ziqiang, and Ma Yilong, Examining Editors; Zhao Qiang, Lan Bi, and Wang Wenbing, Chief Supervising Secretaries; Wang Zhi, Bureau Director; and the Vice Directors …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
臣王叔果臣莊士元而監試
則御史臣黃季瑞臣毛鵬也
巳酉日
陛辭入院廼辛亥甲寅丁巳如
例合諸士三試之拔其儁奉
宸斷取三百人爰錄其名氏併文
二十篇以
===
獻臣璣惟聖王圖治必以興賢
斂才爲急務然士不素養選
之奚從廼其進也不勵以考
課則亦鮮不怠恣者我
皇上紹統中興士偕試南宮者十
有三舉於此蓋彬彬焉得人
稱盛矣而慎作養嚴考課之
alt_text:
臣王〔叔果〕臣汪〔士元〕而監試
則御史臣黃〔季瑞〕臣毛〔鵬〕也
己酉日
陛辭入院迺辛亥甲寅丁巳如
例合諸士三試之拔其儁奉
宸斷取三百人爰錄其名氏并文
二十篇以
===
獻臣璣惟聖王圖治必以興賢
斂才爲急務然士不素養選
之奚從迺其進也不勵以考
課則亦鮮不怠恣者哉
皇上紹統中興士偹試南宮者十
有三舉於此蓋彬彬焉得人
稱盛矣而愼作養嚴考課之
punctuated:
臣王叔果、臣莊士元，而監試則御史臣黃季瑞、臣毛鵬也。巳酉日，陛辭入院，廼辛亥、甲寅、丁巳，如例合諸士三試之，拔其儁，奉宸斷取三百人，爰錄其名氏併文二十篇以獻。
臣璣惟聖王圖治，必以興賢斂才爲急務。然士不素養，選之奚從？廼其進也，不勵以考課，則亦鮮不怠恣者。我皇上紹統中興，士偕試南宮者十有三舉於此，蓋彬彬焉，得人稱盛矣。而慎作養、嚴考課之
translation_en:
…your servants Wang Shuguo and Zhuang Shiyuan; those supervising the examination were the Censors, your servants Huang Jirui and Mao Peng. On the siyou [?] day, we took leave of Your Majesty and entered the examination compound. Then, on the xinhai, jiayin, and dingsi days, we assembled the candidates according to established practice and examined them in three sessions. We selected the outstanding among them and, pursuant to the imperial decision, admitted three hundred men. We accordingly recorded their names, together with twenty essays, for presentation to Your Majesty.
Your servant Ji considers that sage kings, in seeking good government, must make the advancement of the worthy and the gathering of talent their urgent concern. Yet if scholars are not cultivated beforehand, from where can they be selected? And once they have entered service, unless encouraged through assessments of their performance, few will avoid becoming negligent and unrestrained. Since our August Sovereign succeeded to the imperial line and brought about a restoration, there have now been thirteen occasions on which scholars have gathered to sit the Metropolitan Examination at the Ministry of Rites. Cultivated talent has indeed abounded, and the recruitment of worthy men has been acclaimed as flourishing. And his care in nurturing scholars and his rigor in assessing their performance…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
令尤諄切焉海内士莫不承
德思奮誠千載一時之遇也臣誠
不才往以狂瞽之言奉
大對荷蒙
聖恩錄其言似讜拔首一甲讀中
秘叨歷有今官則諸士中遭
幸尤莫如臣者嘗承乏教大
===
===
學顧譾薄無能奉揚
德化成真才每循念瘝曠是懼廼
茲又被
命校文司選士則稱塞尤難為懼
滋深矣於是謹率諸同事誓
心神明冀竭愚誠得人以自
贖凡二十晝夜無敢頃刻遑
alt_text:
令尤諄切焉海內士莫不𣊬
德思奮誠千載一時之遇也臣誠
不才往以狂瞽之言奉
大對荷蒙
聖恩錄其言似讜擢首甲讀中
祕叨歷有今官則諸士中遭
際尤莫如臣者嘗承乏敎大
學顧謭薄無能奉揚
===
德化成眞才每循念鰥曠是懼迺
茲又被
命校文司選士則稱塞尤難爲懼
滋深矣於是謹率諸同事誓
心神明冀竭愚誠得人以自
贖凡二十晝夜無敢頃刻遑
punctuated: 令尤諄切焉。海内士莫不承德思奮，誠千載一時之遇也。臣誠不才，往以狂瞽之言奉大對，荷蒙聖恩，錄其言似讜，拔首一甲，讀中秘，叨歷有今官，則諸士中遭幸尤莫如臣者。嘗承乏教大學，顧譾薄無能奉揚德化，成真才，每循念，瘝曠是懼。廼茲又被命校文司選士，則稱塞尤難，為懼滋深矣。於是謹率諸同事，誓心神明，冀竭愚誠，得人以自贖。凡二十晝夜，無敢頃刻遑
translation_en: …the injunctions are especially earnest and emphatic. Scholars throughout the realm, receiving Your Majesty’s beneficence, all resolve to exert themselves. Truly, this is an opportunity encountered once in a thousand years. Your servant is indeed without talent. Formerly, I presented rash and unenlightened words in response to the great question at the Palace Examination. Favored by Your Majesty’s gracious kindness, my words were accepted as seemingly forthright; I was placed first in the first class and studied in the palace library. Having undeservedly held successive appointments down to my present office, I have enjoyed good fortune unmatched among my fellow scholars. I once served, for want of someone better, as a teacher at the Imperial University. Yet, shallow in learning and ability, I could neither disseminate Your Majesty’s transforming virtue nor develop men of genuine talent. Whenever I reflected on this, I feared that I had neglected my duties. Now I have again received the command to assess examination essays and oversee the selection of scholars. Adequately fulfilling this charge is especially difficult, and my apprehension has grown still deeper. Accordingly, I respectfully led my colleagues in pledging our hearts before the spirits, hoping to exhaust our humble sincerity and redeem my shortcomings by finding worthy men. For twenty days and nights, we dared not take even a moment’s rest…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
息者故事匭卷入必先同試
同試可而後主試者得受冊
覽觀焉臣慮或遺良也語同
試者更搜之棄卷中分閱合
校加詳焉必三試稱衆見僉
同者收之其諸勦說畔經無
當不與也先是戊戌丁未春
===
臣蓋嘗兩濫從事得觀諸士
文然文之盛則未有如今者
言即人人殊而率能發抒所
自得有裨於世用郁乎文哉
信太平之具也斯非
國家菁莪之澤我
皇上久道之所淪洽其何有此而

臣
蓋嘗兩濫從事得觀諸士
文然文之盛則未有如今者
言即人人殊而率能發抒所
自得有裨於世用郁乎文哉
信太平之具也斯非
國家菁莪之澤我
皇上久道之所淪洽其何有此而
punctuated: 息者。故事，匭卷入，必先同試，同試可而後主試者得受冊覽觀焉。臣慮或遺良也，語同試者更搜之棄卷中，分閱合校，加詳焉。必三試稱、衆見僉同者，收之；其諸勦說畔經、無當，不與也。先是戊戌、丁未春，臣蓋嘗兩濫從事，得觀諸士文。然文之盛，則未有如今者。言即人人殊，而率能發抒所自得，有裨於世用。郁乎文哉！信太平之具也。斯非國家菁莪之澤、我皇上久道之所淪洽，其何有此而
translation_en:
…rest. Under established procedure, when the boxed examination scripts arrived, they first had to go to the Associate Examiners. Only after their approval could the Examiners receive the bound scripts and inspect them. Fearing that worthy work might have been overlooked, your servant instructed the Associate Examiners to search again among the rejected scripts, dividing them for reading and comparing their assessments with added care. Only those approved in three reviews [?], with unanimous agreement, were accepted. Those that merely borrowed others’ explanations, departed from the Classics, or lacked substance were not admitted.
Previously, in the springs of the wuxu and dingwei years, your servant had twice had the undeserved privilege of participating in this work and examining the candidates’ compositions. Yet never had their writing flourished as it does today. Though each expressed himself differently, nearly all could articulate insights they had gained for themselves, contributing something useful to the affairs of the world. How splendid their writing! It is indeed an instrument of great peace. Were this not the result of the state’s beneficence in nurturing scholars, and of the pervasive influence of our Emperor’s long adherence to the Way, how could there be such an abundance to …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
能恣臣所擇哉臣用是竊慶
得附以人事君之義可幸奉
詔萬一矣已而徐思曰諸士茲進
必服政中外人將因言責成
也言不復又焉用文之因復
念臣前叨貳留銓亦嘗與聞
考課之典彼其時百司至則
第稽其行孰貴其言者使諸
士異日者不足成其信則所
司將亦奉
國典以繩其後矣即諸士不自
惜主司者將云何矧
皇上天生聖神遐隱必燭臣下行
事莫能欺塞頃以邊臣失
alt_text:
能慫臣所擇哉臣用是竊歎
得附以人事君之義可幸奉
詔萬一矣已而徐思曰諸士茲進
必服政中外人將因言責成
也言不復又焉用文之因復
念臣前叨貳留銓亦嘗與聞
考課之典彼其時百司至則
第稽其行孰貴其言者使諸
士異日者不足成其信則所
===
司將亦奉
國典以繩其後矣即諸士不自
惜主司者將云何劾
皇上天生聖神遐隱必燭臣下行
事莫能盡掩須以遠臣少
punctuated: 能恣臣所擇哉？臣用是竊慶得附以人事君之義，可幸奉詔萬一矣。已而徐思曰：諸士茲進，必服政中外，人將因言責成也。言不復，又焉用文之？因復念臣前叨貳留銓，亦嘗與聞考課之典。彼其時，百司至，則第稽其行，孰貴其言者？使諸士異日者不足成其信，則所司將亦奉國典以繩其後矣。即諸士不自惜，主司者將云何？矧皇上天生聖神，遐隱必燭，臣下行事莫能欺塞。頃以邊臣失
translation_en:
…could there be such ample scope for your servant’s selection? I therefore privately rejoice that I have been able to fulfill something of the duty of serving one’s ruler by recommending worthy men, and may fortunately have carried out one ten-thousandth of the imperial command. Yet afterward, on further reflection, I thought: these scholars, now advancing into office, will surely undertake administrative duties at court and in the provinces. People will demand achievements of them commensurate with their words. If their words are not fulfilled, what use is literary embellishment?

I then recalled that, when I formerly had the undeserved honor of serving as Vice Minister of Personnel in the auxiliary capital, I also participated in the procedures for evaluating officials. At that time, when officials from the various offices arrived, we examined only their conduct; who attached value to their words? If these scholars should hereafter fail to make good their pledges, the responsible authorities will likewise enforce the laws of the state to discipline them. Even if the scholars have no regard for themselves, what will those who presided over their examination have to say?

Moreover, His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with sagely wisdom: even what is remote and hidden is certain to be illuminated by him, and no minister can deceive him or conceal his actions. Recently, owing to failings among the frontier officials…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
懈一時易置殆盡茲歲首又
勅所司察来
覲羣牧嚴汰之中外吏凛凛思
過若將及焉此諸生新進耳
安知其足奉奔走終免於罪
乎斯臣所為諸士懼又以自
懼也但臣所大幸則又有在
===
焉書曰天惟純佑命則商實
詩曰保茲天子生仲山甫今
聖人在上純敬格
天寔篤我
國家以無疆之慶凡
聖心所嚮
天則從之而

安知其足奉奔走終免於罪

懼也但〔臣〕所大幸則又有在

===
聖人在上純敬格
天寔篤我
國家以無疆之慶凡
聖心所嚮
天則從之而
punctuated:
懈，一時易置殆盡。茲歲首，又勅所司察来覲羣牧，嚴汰之。中外吏凛凛思過，若將及焉。此諸生新進耳，安知其足奉奔走，終免於罪乎？斯臣所為諸士懼，又以自懼也。但臣所大幸，則又有在焉。
書曰：「天惟純佑命，則商實。」詩曰：「保茲天子，生仲山甫。」今聖人在上，純敬格天，寔篤我國家以無疆之慶。凡聖心所嚮，天則從之，而
translation_en:
…for negligence, nearly all were replaced at once. At the beginning of this year, he again commanded the responsible authorities to scrutinize the regional administrators coming for court audience and rigorously dismiss the unfit. Officials within and outside the capital trembled and reflected on their faults, as though their own turn were about to come. These candidates are merely newcomers: how can we know whether they will prove equal to diligent service and ultimately escape punishment? This is why your servant fears for these gentlemen and also for himself. Yet your servant has another reason to consider himself most fortunate.
The Book of Documents says: “Heaven wholly supported the mandate, and thus Shang was filled [with worthy men].” The Book of Odes says: “To protect this Son of Heaven, it brought forth Zhong Shanfu.” Now a sage reigns above us; his unalloyed reverence reaches Heaven, which indeed showers our state with boundless blessings. Whatever the sagely heart inclines toward, Heaven follows, and…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
天瑞人符雜然並至此純佑之徵
而詩之所謂保茲者也又安
有
心在求賢而不得賢者哉臣以是
終自慶而願諸士之毋負於
明時也幸相與勗焉
通議大夫吏部右侍郎兼翰
===
林院學士掌詹事府事李璣
謹序

有
心在求賢而不得賢者哉臣以是
終自慶而願諸士之毋負於
明時也幸相與勗焉
通議大夫吏部右侍郎兼翰
林院學士掌詹事府事李〔璣〕
謹序
punctuated:
天瑞人符，雜然並至，此純佑之徵，而詩之所謂保茲者也。又安有心在求賢而不得賢者哉？臣以是終自慶，而願諸士之毋負於明時也。幸相與勗焉。
通議大夫、吏部右侍郎兼翰林院學士、掌詹事府事李璣謹序。
translation_en:
…auspicious signs from Heaven and corresponding portents among men arrive together in profusion. These are evidence of Heaven’s unstinting aid, and what the Book of Odes means by “protecting this ruler.” How, then, could one set one’s heart on seeking worthy men and fail to find them? For this reason, your servant concludes by rejoicing in his good fortune and hoping that all the candidates will prove worthy of this enlightened age. May we encourage one another in this endeavor.
This preface is respectfully composed by Li Ji, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Right Vice Minister of Personnel and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy, administering the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Thirty-eighth Year of Jiajing (1559)

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Wu Shan, Grand Master for Glorious Happiness, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Yuejing; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the yiwei year (1535).

Mao Zan, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Adviser to the Heir Apparent, and Left Vice Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Bangxian; he was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year (1538).

Examiners

Li Ji, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy and administrator of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Bangzai; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Yan Ne, Grand Master for Central Compliance and Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, concurrently Academician and administrator of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Minqing; his registered domicile was Changshu County, Zhili, and he was a native of Wu County. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Associate Examiners

Hu Zhengmeng, Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhengbo; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Jiang Jinhe, Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Jiezhi; he was from Poyang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Lin Lian, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhenheng; he was from Min County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Zhu Dashou, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Attending to Affairs (chengwu lang). His courtesy name was Duanfu; he was from Shanyin County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year (1556).

Cao Dazhang, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Rendering Service (chengshi lang). His courtesy name was Yicheng; he was from Jintan County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Li Gui, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman of the Forest of Literature (wenlin lang). His courtesy name was Tingliang; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Wang Xilie, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Rendering Service (chengshi lang). His courtesy name was Zizhong; his registered domicile was Nanchang County, Jiangxi, and he was a native of Linchuan County. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Zhao Zupeng, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman of the Forest of Literature (wenlin lang). His courtesy name was Zongnan; he was from Dongyang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Chao Li, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Meritorious Service (zhengshi lang). His courtesy name was Junshi; he was from Kai Subprefecture, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Ma Ziqiang, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Attendant Service (congshi lang). His courtesy name was Tiqian; he was from Tong Subprefecture, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Ma Yilong, courtesy name Futu, was a Hanlin Academy Examining Editor with the rank of Gentleman for Service (congshi lang). His place of origin is given as Zhili, □□ [illegible]; he became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the dingwei year (1547).

Zhao Qiang, courtesy name Zizhen, was Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, with the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service (chengshi lang). He was from Yizhou, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Lan Bi, courtesy name Wanqing, was Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service. He was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Wang Wenbing, courtesy name Daochong, was Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for War. He was from Luling County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Wang Zhi, courtesy name Boyong, was Director of the Bureau of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, with the rank of Grand Master for Counsel (fengyi dafu). He was from Hanyang County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year (1544).

Wang Shuguo, courtesy name Yude, was a Secretary serving as Acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Operations in the Ministry of War, with the rank of Gentleman for Upright Service (chengzhi lang). He was from Yongjia County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Zhuang Yingzhen, courtesy name Junpin, was Vice Director of the Zhejiang Bureau in the Ministry of Justice. He was from Jinjiang County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Examination Inspectors:

Huang Jirui, courtesy name Zonghe, was an Investigating Censor for the Shanxi Circuit, with the rank of Gentleman for Literary Service (wenlin lang). He was from Min County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Mao Peng, courtesy name Runan, was an Investigating Censor for the Huguang Circuit, with the rank of Gentleman for Literary Service. He was from Zaoqiang County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Proctors:

Shen Shaoqing, courtesy name Zishan, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Upright Service. He was from Kunshan County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Hu Shiyan, courtesy name Shimei, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Upright Service. He was from Poyang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Bai Qichang, courtesy name Zhaolun, was a Secretary serving as Acting Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue (chengde lang). He was from Wujin County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Xu Wenmian, courtesy name Kesheng, was a Secretary serving as Acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Upright Service. He was from Kaihua County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Officials Responsible for Collecting and Keeping Examination Scripts:

Li Yuan, courtesy name Tiaofu, was a Central Secretariat Drafter with the rank of Gentleman for Summoned Service (zhengshi lang). He was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and was a student admitted by virtue of an official’s status (guansheng).

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Promote the worthy and talented.” He asked, “How can one recognize the worthy and talented so as to promote them?” The Master said, “Promote those you know. As for those you do not know, will others pass them over?”

In virtue, a sage; in exalted position, the Son of Heaven.

Yu and Ji, living in an age of peace, passed their doors three times without entering. Confucius esteemed them as worthy.

Book of Changes (Yijing)

“Supreme good fortune”: being above, there is great cause for rejoicing.

Six in the fourth place: Contentment with restraint brings success. The Image says: “The success of contentment with restraint comes from following the way of the one above.”

The alternation of yin and yang is called the Way. What continues it is goodness; what completes it is inherent nature.

Li means brightness.

Book of Documents (Shujing)

The virtue of cherishing life permeated the hearts of the people.

In serving the spirits of heaven above and earth below, the altars of soil and grain, and the ancestral temples, there was nothing toward which reverence and solemnity were lacking.

May you, Duke, enable me for countless ages to revere Heaven’s favor.

Define anew the boundaries of the capital’s outskirts; carefully secure the territorial defenses, thereby bringing peace to all within the Four Seas.

Book of Odes (Shijing)

王命南仲，往城于方。出車彭彭，旂旐央央。天子命我，城彼朔方。赫赫南仲，玁狁于襄。
聿脩厥德，永言配命，自求多福。
明昭上帝，迄用康年。

春秋
齊侯、衛侯胥命于蒲。桓公三年。公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、齊世子光、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子伐鄭，會于蕭魚。襄公十有一年。
齊人執鄭詹。莊公十有七年。
叔孫豹帥師救晉，次于雍榆。襄公二十有三年。
公會齊侯于夾谷。定公十年。季孫斯、仲孫何忌帥師墮費。定公十有二年。

禮記
天道至教，聖人至德。
translation_en:
We make this spring wine to secure long life.

The king commanded Nan Zhong to go and build fortifications at Fang. The chariots went forth in great numbers, their banners flying splendidly. “The Son of Heaven commands us to fortify that northern region.” Illustrious Nan Zhong drove off the Xianyun.

Cultivate your virtue; ever conform to Heaven’s mandate, and seek abundant blessings for yourself.

The bright and glorious Lord on High at last granted a year of abundance.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The marquis of Qi and the marquis of Wei conferred at Pu. Third year of Duke Huan.
The duke joined the marquis of Jin, the duke of Song, the marquis of Wei, the earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the viscounts of Ju, Zhu, and Teng, the earls of Xue and Qi (杞), and the viscount of Lesser Zhu in attacking Zheng. They assembled at Xiaoyu. Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.

The men of Qi seized Zhan of Zheng. Seventeenth year of Duke Zhuang.

Shusun Bao led an army to relieve Jin and encamped at Yongyu. Twenty-third year of Duke Xiang.

The duke met the marquis of Qi at Jiagu. Tenth year of Duke Ding.
Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led an army to demolish the fortifications of Fei. Twelfth year of Duke Ding.

Book of Rites

The Way of Heaven is the highest teaching; the sage embodies the highest virtue.

擬漢行養老禮詔，永平二年。
擬唐以房玄齡、杜如晦為僕射誥，貞觀三年。
擬含譽瑞星見，輔臣楊士奇進賀詩表，宣德五年。
判語五條：
錢糧互相覺察。
致祭祀典神祇。
不操練軍士。
translation_en:
The Son of Heaven tucks the jade tablet into his girdle, thereby manifesting uprightness to all under Heaven.
All music arises from the human heart. Feelings are stirred within and thus take form in sound; when sounds form patterns, they are called music. Thus, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful, and its government harmonious.
The gui and zhang jade tablets are presented alone and gain admission: this represents virtue.
Second Session
Discourse: The way by which the sage unites the inner and the outer.
One topic from among imperial edicts, proclamations, and memorials [?].
Compose an edict in the manner of the Han dynasty instituting the rites for honoring the aged. Second year of Yongping (59).
Compose a proclamation in the manner of the Tang dynasty appointing Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui as Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs. Third year of Zhenguan (629).
Compose a memorial in the voice of Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi presenting a congratulatory poem on the appearance of the auspicious Hanyu star. Fifth year of Xuande (1430).
Five legal judgments:
Mutual surveillance and reporting concerning money and grain revenues.
Offering sacrifices to deities included in the register of sacrifices.
Failure to train soldiers.

translation_en:
The elderly and the young are not to be interrogated under torture.
Repairing bridges and roads.
Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Question: The Book of Rites says: “Only a sage can offer sacrifice acceptably to the Lord on High.” When sacrifice is offered to the Lord on High at the suburban altar, wind and rain observe their proper measure, and cold and heat arrive in season. Formerly we heard these words; now we have witnessed their magnificent fulfillment. On the winter solstice in the xinmao year of Jiajing, our Emperor offered the burnt sacrifice at the Circular Mound. Within a full month, sweet dew descended upon the burial chamber of his deceased imperial father. That dew should be sweet is an auspicious sign; that it should descend in response to the suburban sacrifice is still more auspicious; that it should descend nowhere else but where the spirit of the deceased imperial father rests is more auspicious yet. We reverently reflect that the deceased imperial father embodied sagacious and discerning virtue, consonant with Heaven’s profound and silent workings. The Lord on High looked upon him with favor, and thus the supreme sage, our Emperor, was born. Where blessings gather in such abundance, auspicious signs issue forth: is this not indeed the natural principle? The deceased imperial father himself once composed verses on sweet dew. His preface said: “Auspicious signs are portents of blessings. Although this sweet dew is formed by the condensation of Heaven’s harmonious vital force, it is in truth that which portends …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
國家之福也乃今福
國家明徵矣
皇考之前知何其神歟非以至誠之故歟禮斗
威儀諸書率稱天瑞繫聖政所致我
皇上乃弗以自居而惟
上帝是戴是祗爰
製記頌名之曰欽
天竊嘗莊誦而繹思之有六義焉有珍佩之誠
焉有申稟之禮焉有稱
===
親之孝焉有撝謙之光焉有子民之仁焉有保
祚之慎焉而要之皆所以欽乎
天夫稽古大聖人莫不欽天聖莫聖於堯尤以
欽稱而甘露亦應之我
皇上與之一揆者也夫堯大難名而成功可見
文章可見我
皇上之精諸士即未易仰窺矣盍觀
煥乎巍然者歟誠能雍容
明盛光揚大澤之博與符瑞之富即康衢謡

===
天夫稽古大聖人莫不欽天聖莫聖於堯堯以
欽稱而甘露亦應之我
皇上與之一揆者也夫堯大難名而成功可見

皇上之精諸士即未易仰窺矣盍觀

明盛光揚大澤之博與符瑞之富即康衢謌
punctuated:
國家之福也。乃今福國家，明徵矣。皇考之前知何其神歟！非以至誠之故歟？《禮斗威儀》諸書率稱天瑞繫聖政所致。我皇上乃弗以自居，而惟上帝是戴是祗，爰製記頌，名之曰《欽天》。竊嘗莊誦而繹思之，有六義焉：有珍佩之誠焉，有申稟之禮焉，有稱親之孝焉，有撝謙之光焉，有子民之仁焉，有保祚之慎焉。而要之，皆所以欽乎天。
夫稽古大聖人，莫不欽天。聖莫聖於堯，尤以欽稱，而甘露亦應之。我皇上與之一揆者也。夫堯大難名，而成功可見，文章可見。我皇上之精，諸士即未易仰窺矣，盍觀煥乎巍然者歟？誠能雍容明盛，光揚大澤之博與符瑞之富，即康衢謡
translation_en:
…the good fortune of the state. Now there is clear proof that it blesses the state. How wondrous was the late imperial father’s foreknowledge! Was this not due to his utmost sincerity? Such works as the Ritual: The Dipper’s Majesty and Ceremonial (Li dou weiyi) generally state that heavenly portents arise from sagely government. Yet our Emperor takes no credit for himself, revering and honoring only the Lord on High. He therefore composed a record and eulogy entitled Revering Heaven (Qin tian). I have reverently recited it and pondered its meaning, finding six principles therein: sincerity in cherishing and taking its lesson to heart; ritual propriety in reporting to Heaven; filial devotion in extolling his father; the radiance of yielding humility; benevolence in treating the people as his children; and vigilance in preserving the imperial succession. In essence, all these serve to revere Heaven.
Now, examining antiquity, we find that all the great sages revered Heaven. None was more sagely than Yao, who was particularly renowned for reverence; sweet dew likewise appeared in response to him. Our Emperor follows the same standard. Yao’s greatness was indeed beyond description, yet his achievements could be seen, and his cultural splendor could be seen. Even if you gentlemen cannot readily discern the refined essence of our Emperor’s virtue, why not contemplate its radiant and towering manifestations? If you can indeed give a dignified account of this enlightened and flourishing age [?], bringing to light the breadth of his great beneficence and the abundance of auspicious signs, then the songs of the broad thoroughfares…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
堯今軼聲焉可也
問頃者
皇上因司牧者不慎聽讞至使小民冤籲乃推
慮天下大矜無辜於是有
勅諭憲臣云都人士無小無大莫不踴躍戴誦
懽然傳之爾諸生不聞之乎
勅中稱古昔帝王及我
祖宗慎重於刑洋洋哉
聖言請遂爾質可乎夫易卦論治獄多取象於
===
離或兼震艮此必有以也而中孚則取
兌巽何也夫舜欽恤尚矣虞書臯陶職
刑何甫刑乃以屬伯夷也夫刑豈祥器
哉而書何祥之也毗庶而罹罰蚩蚩矣
書何以謂之嘉師也是古昔帝王之所
慎重不可不察也夫
太祖寶訓不可殫述述其取喻者喻薅草萊喻
澣垢喻索魚於釡喻射正鵠喻衡鑑喻
漁田喻御喻啖飲食誦之將無不凜然

竟令軼聲焉可也
問頃者
皇上因司牧者不慎聽讞至使小民冤顲乃推
虞天下大狳無辜於是有
勑諭憲臣云都人士無小無大莫不踴躍纂誦
懽然傳之爾諸生不聞之乎
勑中稱古昔帝王及我
祖宗慎重於刑洋洋哉
聖言請遂爾質可乎夫易卦論治獄多取象於
===
離或蕪震艮此必有以也而中孚則取
兊巽何也夫舜欽恤尚矣虞書臯陶職
刑何甫刑乃以屬伯夷也夫刑豈祥器
哉而書何祥之也〔睢庶而懽罰〕嵒嵒矣
書何以謂之嘉師也是古昔帝王之所
慎重不可不察也夫
太祖實訓不可殫述述其取喻者喻嫥草萊喻
瀚垢喻索魚於釜喻射正鵠喻衡鑑喻
漁田喻御喻啖飲食喻之將無不灑然
punctuated:
堯，今軼聲焉可也。

問：頃者，皇上因司牧者不慎聽讞，至使小民冤籲，乃推慮天下，大矜無辜。於是有勅諭憲臣云，都人士無小無大，莫不踴躍戴誦，懽然傳之。爾諸生不聞之乎？勅中稱古昔帝王及我祖宗慎重於刑。洋洋哉，聖言！請遂爾質，可乎？夫《易》卦論治獄，多取象於離，或兼震、艮，此必有以也。而中孚則取兌、巽，何也？夫舜欽恤尚矣，《虞書》臯陶職刑，何《甫刑》乃以屬伯夷也？夫刑豈祥器哉，而《書》何祥之也？毗庶而罹罰，蚩蚩矣，《書》何以謂之嘉師也？是古昔帝王之所慎重，不可不察也。夫《太祖寶訓》不可殫述，述其取喻者：喻薅草萊，喻澣垢，喻索魚於釡，喻射正鵠，喻衡鑑，喻漁田，喻御，喻啖飲食，誦之將無不凜然
translation_en:
…to sing of Yao, now surpassing those earlier songs, would be fitting.

Question: Recently, because those charged with governing the people were careless in hearing and adjudicating cases, causing the common people to cry out against injustice, His Majesty extended his concern throughout the realm and showed great compassion for the innocent. He therefore issued an edict instructing the censorial officials. People in the capital, great and small alike, eagerly and reverently recited it and joyfully passed it on. Have you students not heard it?

The edict speaks of the care that the sovereigns of antiquity and Our imperial ancestors exercised in administering punishments. How profound and expansive are these sagely words! May we now put questions to you concerning them? When the hexagrams of the Book of Changes discuss the adjudication of lawsuits, they mostly draw their imagery from Li, sometimes together with Zhen or Gen. There must be a reason for this. Why, then, does Zhongfu draw on Dui and Xun? Shun’s reverent care and compassion in punishment are indeed venerable precedents. In the Documents of Yu, Gao Yao was responsible for punishments; why, then, does the Punishments of Fu assign this responsibility to Bo Yi? Are punishments auspicious instruments? Why does the Book of Documents describe them as auspicious? The common people [?] who incur punishment are ignorant; why does the Book of Documents call them the “good multitude”? These are matters to which the sovereigns of antiquity gave careful attention, and they must be examined.

The Precious Instructions of Taizu cannot be recounted exhaustively. Let us recount those that employ analogies: weeding out wild growth; washing away dirt; seeking fish in a cooking pot; shooting at the center of a target; scales and mirrors; fishing and farming [?]; driving a carriage; and eating and drinking. Those who recite these will surely all be filled with awe…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
者
成祖諭薛嵓陳瑛吳盛執法諸臣綦惓惓也是
我
祖宗之所慎重不可不欽念也夫不察不欽念
是故多莽鹵於為政而土芥其民如
勅中所云此豈仰稱
皇上好生之德哉爾方從閭閻來熟識司牧者
情狀將必皆曰
天子至神聖誠明見千萬里外然不知
===
勅中申飭之旨司牧者能一一省否也夫木鐸
徇道路將以聳聽故欲爾恭按
勅旨大闡悉之以致丁寧於司牧者
問風俗關於天下至重也故自昔帝王皆
以教化為首務而其時道德一風俗同
者有以焉然其所以為之教者可得而
聞歟三代以降民俗士風載在史冊炳
如也終未有若三代之隆者何哉豈古
今人不相及歟抑淳樸漸漓卒不可還

狥道路將以聳聽故欲爾恭按
勑旨大闡悉之以致丁寧於司牧者

者有以焉然其所以爲之教者可得而

如也終未有若三代之隆者何哉豈古
今人不相及歟抑淳樸漸漓卒不可逻
punctuated:
者。
成祖諭薛嵓、陳瑛、吳盛執法諸臣，綦惓惓也。是我祖宗之所慎重，不可不欽念也。夫不察、不欽念，是故多莽鹵於為政，而土芥其民，如勅中所云。此豈仰稱皇上好生之德哉？爾方從閭閻來，熟識司牧者情狀，將必皆曰：「天子至神聖，誠明見千萬里外。」然不知勅中申飭之旨，司牧者能一一省否也。夫木鐸徇道路，將以聳聽，故欲爾恭按勅旨，大闡悉之，以致丁寧於司牧者。
問：風俗關於天下至重也，故自昔帝王皆以教化為首務，而其時道德一、風俗同者，有以焉。然其所以為之教者，可得而聞歟？三代以降，民俗士風載在史冊，炳如也。終未有若三代之隆者，何哉？豈古今人不相及歟？抑淳樸漸漓，卒不可還
translation_en:
…who would not be filled with awe.
Chengzu’s admonitions to Xue Yan, Chen Ying, Wu Sheng, and the other ministers charged with enforcing the law were most earnest. These were matters that our imperial ancestors treated with great care; we must contemplate them reverently. Failure to examine these matters and contemplate them reverently thus leads to much reckless conduct in government and to treating the people as dirt and weeds, as the edict says. How could this accord with His Majesty’s virtue of cherishing life? You have just come from among the common people and know well the circumstances and conduct of those who govern them. Surely you will all say: “The Son of Heaven is supremely sagely; truly, he sees clearly what happens thousands upon thousands of li away.” Yet we do not know whether those who govern the people can take to heart, point by point, the admonitions in the edict. A wooden-tongued bell is carried along the roads to command people’s attention. Accordingly, we wish you reverently to examine the edict’s purport and expound it fully, so that its earnest admonitions may reach those who govern the people.
Question: Customs are of the utmost importance to the realm. Thus, from antiquity, emperors and kings have all made moral instruction their foremost task. There were reasons why moral principles were unified and customs uniform in their times. But may we hear how they carried out this instruction? Since the Three Dynasties, the customs of the people and the conduct of scholars have been recorded with clarity in the histories. Why has there ultimately never been anything to equal the flourishing conditions of the Three Dynasties? Is it that people today cannot measure up to those of antiquity? Or has simple integrity gradually been diluted, so that it can never be restored…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
諸古歟昔荀悅庾澄皆有感於時著為
疏論其言亦有可采者歟悅謂先屏四
患乃崇五政澄謂不足懼者五深可畏
者六夫所謂四患六畏者不知何指也
其要亦有所歸歟
國初風俗淳美民節儉士正直足以比隆三
代矣迄于今則漸不能以無異抑有如
悅之所患澄之所畏者歟
聖天子在上壽考作人將以移風易俗而
===
詔旨屢廑天下士民猶未盡復諸舊者其故何
哉豈亦有司奉行
德意者猶有所未至歟諸士固斯民之秀也攷
古驗今必有能得其故者願明以告我
問自古明君必重治民之官而於所最親
民者尤重焉則守令是已守令稱良惟
漢世為盛可舉而評之乎其所敘述惟
曰謹身帥先居以廉平至於明發奸伏
吏端禁止者乃不滿焉然則吏之所為

吏端禁止者乃不滿焉然則吏之所爲
punctuated:
諸古歟？昔荀悅、庾澄皆有感於時，著為疏論，其言亦有可采者歟？悅謂先屏四患，乃崇五政；澄謂不足懼者五，深可畏者六。夫所謂四患六畏者，不知何指也？其要亦有所歸歟？國初風俗淳美，民節儉，士正直，足以比隆三代矣。迄于今，則漸不能以無異，抑有如悅之所患、澄之所畏者歟？聖天子在上，壽考作人，將以移風易俗，而詔旨屢廑，天下士民猶未盡復諸舊者，其故何哉？豈亦有司奉行德意者猶有所未至歟？諸士固斯民之秀也，攷古驗今，必有能得其故者，願明以告我。

問：自古明君必重治民之官，而於所最親民者尤重焉，則守令是已。守令稱良，惟漢世為盛，可舉而評之乎？其所敘述，惟曰謹身帥先，居以廉平；至於明發奸伏、吏端禁止者，乃不滿焉。然則吏之所為
translation_en:
…to antiquity? In former times, Xun Yue and Yu Cheng, each moved by the circumstances of his age, composed memorials and discourses. Is there anything in their words worth adopting? Yue maintained that one must first eliminate the four evils and then promote the five measures of government; Cheng maintained that there were five things insufficient to cause fear and six things deeply to be dreaded. What, we ask, did these so-called four evils and six objects of dread refer to? Did their essential arguments converge on some common point?

At the beginning of our dynasty, customs were pure and excellent: the people were frugal, and scholars upright, sufficiently so to rival the flourishing Three Dynasties. By the present day, however, differences have gradually become unavoidable. Might there be conditions such as those Yue regarded as evils and Cheng dreaded? The sage Son of Heaven reigns above, enjoying longevity and nurturing men of talent, intent on transforming prevailing practices and customs. Yet although he has repeatedly taken pains to issue edicts, the scholars and common people throughout the realm have still not fully returned to their former ways. Why is this? Could it also be that the responsible officials have not fully carried out his benevolent intentions? You scholars are indeed the finest among these people. In examining antiquity and testing it against the present, surely some of you can discover the reasons. I ask you to explain them clearly to me.

Question: Since antiquity, enlightened rulers have invariably attached importance to officials who govern the people, and especially to those in closest contact with them—namely, prefects and magistrates. It was particularly during the Han that prefects and magistrates renowned for good government flourished. Can you cite and assess examples? The accounts of them speak only of their being circumspect in their own conduct, leading by example, and holding office with integrity and impartiality. As for those who astutely exposed concealed wrongdoing and ‘official abuses and prohibitions’ [?], these accounts express dissatisfaction with them. Then, as for what makes an official…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄

良果在彼不在此耶
聖天子加意百姓簡賢使能為守若令者誠宜
宣布
德意於民然猶澤不下究民或愁嘆將吏未盡
良而撫字之道多未至歟夫士自一命
以上存心愛物必有所濟乃今所稱良
雖漢龔黃不為讓至責求實效則鮮有
濟焉豈采名不采實今亦有是弊歟而
吏遂緣是炫飾虛聲顧罔實是務也茲

而後可
問井田之制不復則兵不得不養於官然
歷代之初皆兵民兩便鮮不贍足者乃
其後顧往往稱乏焉即如建武熙豐間
武事不競思振之則其處財給費似不
容已者而論者咎焉豈其事固有本末
而當時所以行之者非歟我
朝兵有定籍賦有定法赫然稱富強久矣□

而當時所以行之者非歟抑
朝兵有定籍賦有定法赫然稱富強久矣顧
punctuated:
良果在彼不在此耶？聖天子加意百姓，簡賢使能，為守若令者誠宜宣布德意於民。然猶澤不下究，民或愁嘆，將吏未盡良，而撫字之道多未至歟？夫士自一命以上，存心愛物，必有所濟。乃今所稱良，雖漢龔黃不為讓，至責求實效，則鮮有濟焉。豈采名不采實，今亦有是弊歟？而吏遂緣是炫飾虛聲，顧罔實是務也。茲欲使吏循民安，天下共登諸理，必何施而後可？

問：井田之制不復，則兵不得不養於官。然歷代之初，皆兵民兩便，鮮不贍足者；乃其後，顧往往稱乏焉。即如建武、熙豐間，武事不競，思振之，則其處財給費似不容已者，而論者咎焉。豈其事固有本末，而當時所以行之者非歟？我朝兵有定籍，賦有定法，赫然稱富強久矣。□
translation_en:
…does excellence in office truly lie in the former rather than the latter? The sagely Son of Heaven gives special attention to the common people, selecting the worthy and employing the capable. Those serving as prefects or magistrates should indeed make his benevolent intentions known to the people. Yet his beneficence still does not reach all the way down, and some among the people grieve and lament. Is this because the officials are not all good, and their ways of tending and nurturing the people remain inadequate in many respects? Any man holding even the lowest official appointment, if he sets his heart on caring for others, must accomplish some good. Yet those now acclaimed as good officials are said to yield nothing even to Gong Sui and Huang Ba of the Han; when actual results are demanded, however, few have accomplished anything. Could the fault of valuing reputation rather than substance exist today as well? Officials consequently exploit this to embellish their hollow reputations, making disregard for substance their business. If we now wish officials to govern conscientiously, the people to live in peace, and all under Heaven to attain good order together, what measures must we take to achieve this?

Question: Since the well-field system has not been restored, troops must necessarily be maintained by the government. Yet at the beginning of successive dynasties, arrangements benefited both soldiers and civilians, and resources were seldom insufficient. Later, however, shortages were frequently reported. Take, for example, the Jianwu reign and the Xining and Yuanfeng reigns: military affairs were languishing, and efforts were made to revive them. Securing funds and meeting expenses would seem to have been unavoidable, yet commentators condemned these measures. Was this because such matters inherently have roots and branches—fundamentals and secondary concerns—and the methods used at the time were mistaken? Under our dynasty, troops have established registers and taxation has established rules; we have long been renowned for wealth and strength. [?] …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
以南北邊吏失戒倭虜奄入然□□
不敵吾遠甚此不足為大憂者而當事
者即苦於兵費不給疏請紛然司計者
不得已至出一切權宜之術破諸格佐
之然且告匱未已不知後是又何所繼
也或謂聚財莫若省財今之財大率耗
於兵冗而不可使戰其道莫如簡兵練
土著二說行則召募調遣可罷財益可
省信歟或又謂利久遠須復屯田修塩
===
法乃議者則謂屯田兼併難清私販難
革二法卒不行然乎否乎茲必修復之
其道安在諸士抱業而来行且試於政
事矣其於天下之務宜必有概於中也
主司以俊傑為望幸無讓焉

不得已至出一切權宜之術破諸格佐

省信歟或又謂利久遠須復屯田修塩
法乃議者則謂屯田兼併難清私販難
革二法卒不行然乎否乎茲必修復之
其道安在諸士抱業而來行且試於政
事矣其於天下之務宜必有槩於中也
主司以俊傑爲望幸無讓焉
punctuated: 以南北邊吏失戒，倭虜奄入，然□□不敵吾遠甚，此不足為大憂者。而當事者即苦於兵費不給，疏請紛然；司計者不得已，至出一切權宜之術，破諸格佐之，然且告匱未已，不知後是又何所繼也。或謂聚財莫若省財，今之財大率耗於兵冗而不可使戰，其道莫如簡兵、練土著。二說行，則召募調遣可罷，財益可省，信歟？或又謂利久遠須復屯田、修塩法，乃議者則謂屯田兼併難清，私販難革，二法卒不行，然乎否乎？茲必修復之，其道安在？諸士抱業而来，行且試於政事矣，其於天下之務，宜必有概於中也。主司以俊傑為望，幸無讓焉。
translation_en:
…because the frontier officials in the south and north failed to maintain vigilance, Japanese raiders and northern foes suddenly invaded. Yet their □□ fall far short of ours [?], so this is not cause for great concern. Those responsible, however, immediately found themselves short of funds for military expenses, and memorials requesting assistance poured in. Those administering the finances had no alternative but to resort to every expedient, setting aside established regulations to provide support. Even so, shortages continue to be reported, and we do not know how expenditure can be sustained hereafter.

Some say that accumulating funds is less effective than economizing. At present, funds are largely consumed by troops who are excessive in number yet cannot be put into battle. The best course would therefore be to select the troops and train local inhabitants. If these two proposals were implemented, recruitment and the dispatch of troops could cease, and further savings could be made. Is this true?

Others say that lasting benefits require restoring military agricultural colonies and reforming the salt administration. Those discussing these proposals, however, maintain that the engrossment of colony lands is difficult to remedy and illicit salt trading difficult to eradicate; consequently, neither measure is put into effect. Is this so or not? If these institutions must now be reformed and restored, how should this be done?

You gentlemen have come equipped with your learning and will soon be put to the test in government affairs. You surely ought to have formed some considered views on the business of the realm. The presiding examiners look to you as men of outstanding talent; we hope you will not hold back.

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
舉賢才曰焉知賢才而舉之曰舉爾所知
爾所不知人其舍諸
林奇材
同考試官員外郎莊批此作不牽俗套於聖
人用人意思發揮殆盡可以觀所養矣
同考試官都給事中王批此題作者類浮冗可
厭是篇獨簡潔峻拔其真所謂賢才者耶
===
同考試官修撰諸批渾厚莊雅而發揮明
盡非識高學粹者不能宜錄為式
同考試官侍讀姜批造詞嚴整而意更渾
融文之最優者尤宜錄矣
考試官學士嚴批其意邃其詞勁是超凡
之作也
考試官學士李批理明詞鬯可錄
聖人啓賢者以用人而因曉其所以盡得乎人
焉夫用人為政之要也而合人己以為公又何

第壹場

四書

舉賢才。曰：「焉知賢才而舉之？」曰：「舉爾所知，爾所不知，人其舍諸？」

林奇材

同考試官員外郎莊批：「此作不牽俗套，於聖人用人意思發揮殆盡，可以觀所養矣。」

同考試官都給事中王批：「此題作者類浮冗可厭，是篇獨簡潔峻拔，其真所謂賢才者耶？」

同考試官修撰諸批：「渾厚莊雅，而發揮明盡，非識高學粹者不能，宜錄為式。」

同考試官侍讀姜批：「造詞嚴整，而意更渾融，文之最優者，尤宜錄矣。」

考試官學士嚴批：「其意邃，其詞勁，是超凡之作也。」

考試官學士李批：「理明詞鬯，可錄。」

聖人啓賢者以用人，而因曉其所以盡得乎人焉。夫用人為政之要也，而合人己以為公，又何
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Raise worthy and talented men to office.” He asked, “How can I recognize worthy and talented men and raise them to office?” The Master replied, “Raise those you know. As for those you do not know, would others pass them over?”

Lin Qicai

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhuang, Vice Director: “This composition is not constrained by conventional formulas. It expounds almost fully the sage’s intentions concerning the employment of men, revealing the author’s cultivation.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Those who write on this topic are generally superficial and prolix, to a tiresome degree. This essay alone is concise, lucid, and outstanding. Is its author not truly one of those called worthy and talented?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Senior Compiler: “Substantial, dignified, and elegant, it expounds the subject clearly and fully. Only someone of lofty discernment and refined learning could accomplish this. It should be included as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Reader-in-waiting: “Its phrasing is rigorous and orderly, while its ideas are even more fully integrated. It is among the finest compositions and particularly deserves inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: “Its ideas are profound and its language vigorous. This is a work that transcends the ordinary.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: “Its reasoning is clear and its language fluent. It merits inclusion.”

The sage instructed a worthy man in employing men and thereby explained to him how to secure the services of all suitable men. Employing men is essential to government; and when one combines the judgment of others with one’s own to achieve impartiality, what further…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
患於人之不知且舉哉夫子所以答仲弓者如
此若曰先有司而赦小過宰之當務者固也而
不急於用人其可乎故爾當知夫國之須於賢
才者甚殷而必盡乎汲引之道人之關於進退
者甚重而務合乎舉用之宜以厚俗者尚乎賢
賢者則舉之在位而在我不可使有蔽賢之譏
也以修政者存乎才才者則舉之在職而在人
不可使有遺才之嘆也斯則有司得人以充而
在人由我以倡固有賢才畢舉而不患於不知
===
者乃仲弓不悟而曰焉知賢才而舉之是無見
於人己合一之公矣故夫子則從而廣之蓋以
為取必於己者隘而同人無我者明賢才之伏
於下也爾固難於徧知之矣而爾豈無有已知
者乎爾之於賢才也誠有所不及知者矣而人
豈遂無知之者乎爾所知者爾從而舉之而其
所未知者則姑以付之於人也是何也薦賢雖
義之急而限於知焉事之不容強者則然耳由

translation_en:
…why worry that worthy men will not be recognized and recommended? This was how the Master answered Zhonggong, as if to say: “Taking the lead among the responsible officials and pardoning minor faults are certainly pressing duties for an administrator. Yet can he fail to make employing men a priority? You should therefore understand that the state's need for worthy and talented men is exceedingly urgent, and that every means of drawing them into service must be exhausted. Advancing or withdrawing from office is a matter of great consequence for men, so recommendations and appointments must be made appropriately. To enrich public customs, esteem worthiness: recommend worthy men for positions, so that you yourself incur no reproach for concealing the worthy. To put government in order, rely on talent: recommend talented men for offices, so that others have no cause to lament that talent has been overlooked. Thus the offices will be filled with suitable men, and others will follow the lead I provide. All worthy and talented men can indeed be recommended, without any need to worry that they will remain unknown.”
Yet Zhonggong did not understand and asked: “How can I recognize worthy and talented men and recommend them?” This showed that he did not perceive the impartiality that unites oneself and others. The Master therefore broadened his understanding. His meaning was that insisting on relying entirely upon oneself is narrow-minded, whereas joining with others without self-centeredness is clear-sighted. As worthy and talented men remain hidden in humble stations, you certainly cannot easily know them all. But surely there are some whom you already know? Among the worthy and talented, there are indeed some beyond your knowledge. But does that mean no one else knows them? Recommend those whom you know, and for the time being entrust those whom you do not know to others. Why is this? Although recommending the worthy is an urgent moral duty, it is limited by one's knowledge: this is simply a matter in which one cannot force what is beyond one's power. Accordingly, others will recommend those whom they know; and as for those beyond your knowledge, others…

豈終於舍之乎？又何也？好善，則人之間善為之倡焉，心之不容已者固然耳。是其始也，有所舉，有所不及舉，在我若限於未知；而其終也，因所知及於所未知，在人不患於不舉，尚何不知之足慮也哉？抑進賢如不得已，軻之言又若不專任之人者，何耶？蓋下之舉賢貴於廣，而上之用賢貴於慎；不慎而廣，以言乎失，則均也。是故迪知忱恂，然後九德用；而非其人，則官寧有不備。三代慎於用人者固如此。雖然，九官十二牧之命，必極於疇咨，則所謂進賢如不得已者，又豈獨三代之道為然哉？
德為聖人，尊為天子。
蔡茂春

translation_en:
…would they ever leave such men aside? Why, moreover, is this so? When one loves goodness, goodness among people finds a champion in him [?]; this is simply because the heart cannot restrain itself. Thus, at first, there are men one recommends and others one has not managed to recommend: on one’s own part, one seems constrained by what one does not know. In the end, however, through those who are known, one reaches those who were unknown; with others involved, there is no fear that they will go unrecommended. What cause remains to worry about not knowing them?
Yet Meng Ke’s statement that one should advance worthy men as though compelled to do so seems to suggest that this should not be entrusted entirely to others. Why is this? In recommending worthy men, those below should prize breadth; in employing worthy men, those above should prize caution. To seek breadth without caution is equally an error. Thus, only after truly ascertaining their sincerity and trustworthiness were men possessing the nine virtues employed; if the right men were lacking, offices were preferably left unfilled. Such indeed was the caution with which the Three Dynasties employed men. Nevertheless, appointments to the nine offices and the twelve regional governorships necessarily involved the fullest consultation. How, then, could advancing worthy men as though compelled to do so have been a principle peculiar to the Three Dynasties?
“In virtue, a sage; in exalted station, the Son of Heaven.”
Cai Maochun

觀虞聖德位之至，而孝之大徵矣。夫孝子莫大於尊顯其親也，而舜德位兼至焉，則所以成其孝者孰踰乎？夫子以大孝稱舜，而此著其實，若曰：孝者，庸德也，而舜所以爲大者何哉？蓋以欲顯親者存乎德，而德非聖人，則顯矣而非其至也。乃舜之德則爲聖人焉。觀其樂取之誠，舜固未嘗自居其聖者。然濬哲中涵，精一啓心學之秘，倫物察而非有所思也；温恭外著，重華協帝德之明，仁義由而非有所勉也。是以天下法之，
translation_en:
…It brings out the sage’s filial devotion in honoring his parents and making them illustrious, with a clarity that invites recitation.
Associate Examiner Wang, a Compiler, comments: Most writers can discuss how the great Shun honored his parents and made them illustrious. This essay alone traces this back to his disposition never to regard himself as a sage or as exalted. It particularly reveals learning with deep roots.
Associate Examiner Li, a Compiler, comments: It elucidates almost fully how the great Shun honored his parents and made them illustrious. Only a seasoned scholar could attain this.
Examiner Yan, an Academician, comments: Its accounts of Shun’s virtue and position alike avoid worn-out expressions and show insight.
Examiner Li, an Academician, comments: Clear and incisive.
Observe the consummate virtue and position of the sage of Yu, and the greatness of his filial devotion becomes manifest. For a filial son, nothing is greater than honoring his parents and making them illustrious. Since Shun attained the utmost in both virtue and position, who could surpass him in fulfilling filial devotion? The Master praised Shun for his great filial devotion, and here sets forth its substance, as though saying: Filial devotion is an ordinary virtue; why, then, was Shun’s called great? Making one’s parents illustrious depends upon virtue. Yet if one’s virtue falls short of sagehood, one may make them illustrious without doing so to the highest degree. Shun’s virtue, however, was that of a sage. Consider the sincerity with which he delighted in adopting what was good in others: Shun certainly never regarded himself as a sage. Yet profound wisdom dwelt within him; his refinement and singleness of purpose disclosed the mysteries of the learning of the mind. He discerned human relationships and the affairs of things without needing deliberation. Gentleness and reverence shone outwardly; his renewed splendor accorded with the brilliance of the emperor’s virtue. He followed benevolence and righteousness without needing exertion. Thus all under Heaven took him as their model …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
後世傳焉雖有作者而舜為弗可及矣夫德則
歸舜而本其篤生之自則有貽之以名而名由
以無窮者舜非顯親之至而何哉欲尊親者存
乎位而位非天子則尊矣而非其至也乃舜之
尊則為天子焉觀其南河之遜舜固未嘗自期
於位者然帝王曆數天心默定於受終主祭而
神享之也朝覲謳歌人心久歸於歷試治事而
民安之也是以中國踐焉元后陟焉雖有爵者
而舜為弗可上矣夫尊則歸舜而展其報本之
===
誠則有從之以尊而尊由以特異者舜非尊親
之至而何哉況乎德之所在而位天子焉則德
以位而益顯位之所在而德聖人焉則位以德
而益尊此舜所以成孝之大而人子無復可用
其情矣其孰得而及之哉嘗讀二典而於舜有
深慕焉舜以聖德居天子之位有虞風動而萬
世之下頌其治者不衰則信乎聖人之盛而立
君道之極者夫子嘗曰君哉帝舜又豈非觀於
上世之化而獨有所嘉者乎然則舜盖配天之

punctuated: 後世傳焉，雖有作者，而舜為弗可及矣。夫德則歸舜，而本其篤生之自，則有貽之以名，而名由以無窮者。舜非顯親之至而何哉？欲尊親者存乎位，而位非天子，則尊矣而非其至也。乃舜之尊則為天子焉。觀其南河之遜，舜固未嘗自期於位者。然帝王曆數，天心默定於受終，主祭而神享之也；朝覲謳歌，人心久歸於歷試，治事而民安之也。是以中國踐焉，元后陟焉，雖有爵者，而舜為弗可上矣。夫尊則歸舜，而展其報本之誠，則有從之以尊，而尊由以特異者。舜非尊親之至而何哉？況乎德之所在而位天子焉，則德以位而益顯；位之所在而德聖人焉，則位以德而益尊。此舜所以成孝之大，而人子無復可用其情矣，其孰得而及之哉？嘗讀二典，而於舜有深慕焉。舜以聖德居天子之位，有虞風動，而萬世之下頌其治者不衰，則信乎聖人之盛而立君道之極者。夫子嘗曰：「君哉，帝舜！」又豈非觀於上世之化而獨有所嘉者乎？然則舜盖配天之
translation_en:
…and later generations transmit his example. Even should others arise, Shun cannot be equaled. Although this virtue belongs to Shun, when we trace the source from which so exceptional a man was born, we find that he bestows renown upon his parents, and through him their renown becomes inexhaustible. How could Shun be anything but the supreme example of bringing distinction to one’s parents?

To confer honor upon one’s parents depends upon one’s position. If that position is not that of the Son of Heaven, one may honor them, but not to the utmost degree. Shun’s exalted position, however, was that of the Son of Heaven. Consider his withdrawal to the south of the Yellow River: Shun certainly never presumed that he would occupy the throne. Yet Heaven’s succession of emperors and kings was silently settled in its heart when he received the transfer of rule: he presided over sacrifices, and the spirits accepted them. Through court audiences and songs of praise, the people’s hearts had long turned toward him during his successive trials in office: he administered affairs, and the people enjoyed peace. Thus he assumed the throne in the central realm and ascended to supreme sovereignty. Though others might possess noble rank, none could stand above Shun. Although this exalted status belongs to Shun, when he gives full expression to his sincerity in repaying his origins, his parents share in his honor, and through him their honor becomes exceptional. How could Shun be anything but the supreme example of honoring one’s parents?

Moreover, when one possesses such virtue and occupies the position of the Son of Heaven, that position makes one’s virtue still more manifest. When one occupies such a position and possesses the virtue of a sage, that virtue makes one’s position still more exalted. This is how Shun brought filial piety to its full greatness, leaving no further scope for a son to express his devotion. Who could equal him?

I have read the Two Canons and felt profound admiration for Shun. With a sage’s virtue, Shun occupied the position of the Son of Heaven, and the realm of Yu responded as though moved by the wind. Even ten thousand generations later, praise of his government has not diminished. Truly, he possessed the fullness of sagehood and established the highest standard of the ruler’s Way. The Master once said: “What a ruler Emperor Shun was!” Was this not also a judgment made upon observing the transforming influence of ancient times and finding in him particular cause for praise? Thus Shun surely possessed a governance matching Heaven’s …

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Chief Supervising Secretary: To obtain the right opportunity and put the Way into practice—this is why Confucius esteemed Yu and Ji as worthy. This essay grasps the point with genuine understanding and precision. Its author must aspire to serve the world. It should be included as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Examining Editor: Throughout his life, Mencius took Confucius as his standard of judgment. The precise reason Confucius esteemed Yu and Ji as worthy was that, encountering favorable times, they worked diligently at their duties. Candidates in the examination hall fail to grasp this; their essays repeat one another and follow hackneyed precedents, making them thoroughly tiresome to read. Of late, examination studies have greatly deteriorated. Students devote themselves exclusively to memorizing stale formulas, seeking the advantage of examination success; there is no longer any investigation of principle or substantive learning. This essay brings out the meaning of Mencius’s words and is therefore included as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor: Its account of Yu and Ji’s urgency in saving the people is precise and apt, and it is especially perceptive in grasping the meaning of “esteemed them as worthy.” Include it.

考試官學士李批詞古意透是體禹稷之心
者
聖臣遇時而勤事聖人之所與也夫聖人之道
與時偕行者也孔子之賢禹稷也非以其時之
既遇而克勤其事哉今夫濟天下以道行道以
時時行而行吾於禹稷見之矣禹稷所當之時
何時也唐虞之際貞元會而聖作堯舜之聖上
下交而志同盖洪水艱食天下雖若猶未平也
===

聖臣遇時而勤事，聖人之所與也。夫聖人之道，與時偕行者也。孔子之賢禹稷也，非以其時之既遇而克勤其事哉？今夫濟天下以道，行道以時，時行而行，吾於禹稷見之矣。禹稷所當之時，何時也？唐虞之際，貞元會而聖作；堯舜之聖，上下交而志同。盖洪水艱食，天下雖若猶未平也，而君明臣良，天下有所賴以平也，是平世也。禹稷當其時，因當其任；當其任，因當其事。禹爲司空，四載是乘，而盡力於荒度，日孜孜焉，必使九州攸同、四隩既宅而後已也，三過其門不入也。稷爲農師，百穀是播，而躬敎乎稼穡，日孜孜焉，必使烝民乃粒、萬邦作乂而後已也，三過其門不入也。夫過門且不入，則非過門之時可知已；三過門三不入，則久於其外可知已。禹稷之勤其官於平世也如此，孔子何以賢之耶？禹稷所

…in his own time. Select this answer.
Examiner, Academician Li, comments: “The language is antique and the meaning penetrating. This writer grasps the hearts of Yu and Ji.”
When sagely ministers encounter a favorable age and diligently perform their duties, they earn the sage’s approval. For the sage’s Way proceeds in step with the times. Was it not because Yu and Ji encountered their proper time and diligently fulfilled their responsibilities that Confucius esteemed them? Now, one delivers the world through the Way and puts the Way into practice as the times permit. Acting when the time calls for action: this is what I see in Yu and Ji. What sort of age did they encounter? In the age of Tang and Yu, the cycle’s end met its beginning and sages arose. With the sage rulers Yao and Shun, those above and below were in communion and shared one purpose. Floods and scarcity of food made the world seem still unsettled; yet with enlightened rulers and worthy ministers, the world had those upon whom it could rely for peace. This was an age of peace. Encountering this age, Yu and Ji accordingly assumed its responsibilities; assuming those responsibilities, they accordingly undertook its tasks. Yu served as Minister of Works. Using the four kinds of conveyance, he devoted all his strength to surveying the land, laboring diligently day after day. He would stop only when the Nine Provinces were brought into order together and the lands in all four quarters were made habitable. Three times he passed his own gate without entering. Ji served as Master of Agriculture. He sowed the hundred grains and personally taught the people to plant and reap, laboring diligently day after day. He would stop only when the multitude had grain to eat and the myriad states were brought into order. Three times he passed his own gate without entering. If they would not enter even when passing their gates, we can infer how they acted when they were not passing them. If they passed their gates three times and did not enter on any occasion, we can infer how long they remained away from home. Such was Yu and Ji’s diligence in office in an age of peace. title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
行之道孔子之所欲行也禹稷所遇之時孔子
之所欲遇也禹稷當堯舜之世而時可以行其
行之而勤也是樂則行之之義孔子以爲濟世
當如是也孔子不能遇禹稷之時而慕其道之
得行其賢之也是用之則行之志孔子所爲曠
世而相感也吾無間然以賢禹而書若詩述之
天下爲烈以賢稷而書若詩述之孔子固有以
哉是則禹稷心堯舜之心而堯舜之世益平孔
子心禹稷之心而禹稷之賢以彰故曰先聖後
===
聖其揆一也抑又論之居陋巷之顏子異於過
門不入之禹稷矣而孔子亦賢之賢其能相時
也夫顏子相時而居陋巷焉無禹稷之遇也而
禹稷之遇則遇堯舜也禹稷遇堯舜而得以賢
稱是禹稷之賢堯舜成之也堯舜能成禹稷之
賢是故禹稷則孔子賢之堯舜則孔子聖之
易
元吉在上大有慶也
黃國華

子心禹稷之心而禹稷之賢以彰故曰先聖後
===

賢是故禹稷則孔子賢之堯舜則孔子聖之

元吉在上大有慶也
黄國華
punctuated:
行之道，孔子之所欲行也；禹稷所遇之時，孔子之所欲遇也。禹稷當堯舜之世，而時可以行，其行之而勤也，是樂則行之之義，孔子以爲濟世當如是也。孔子不能遇禹稷之時，而慕其道之得行，其賢之也，是用之則行之志，孔子所爲曠世而相感也。「吾無間然」，以賢禹，而《書》若《詩》述之；「天下爲烈」，以賢稷，而《書》若《詩》述之。孔子固有以哉！是則禹稷心堯舜之心，而堯舜之世益平；孔子心禹稷之心，而禹稷之賢以彰。故曰：「先聖後聖，其揆一也。」抑又論之，居陋巷之顏子，異於過門不入之禹稷矣，而孔子亦賢之，賢其能相時也。夫顏子相時而居陋巷焉，無禹稷之遇也；而禹稷之遇，則遇堯舜也。禹稷遇堯舜而得以賢稱，是禹稷之賢，堯舜成之也。堯舜能成禹稷之賢，是故禹稷則孔子賢之，堯舜則孔子聖之。
《易》
元吉在上，大有慶也。
黃國華
translation_en:
…the Way they practiced was what Kongzi wished to practice; the age that Yu and Ji encountered was what Kongzi wished to encounter. Yu and Ji lived in the age of Yao and Shun, when circumstances permitted them to act. Their diligence in acting exemplified the principle of acting when circumstances were favorable. Kongzi believed that this was how one ought to bring relief to the world. Unable to encounter an age like theirs, Kongzi admired the opportunity they had to put their Way into practice. His esteem for their worth expressed his resolve to act if employed: this was how he felt an affinity with them across distant ages. “I can find no fault” praises Yu’s worth, and the Book of Documents and the Book of Odes recount it; “his achievements extended throughout the realm” praises Ji’s worth, and the Book of Documents and the Book of Odes recount it. Kongzi certainly had grounds for his judgment! Thus Yu and Ji took the hearts of Yao and Shun as their own, and the age of Yao and Shun became still more peaceful; Kongzi took the hearts of Yu and Ji as his own, and their worth thereby became manifest. Hence the saying: “The sages of earlier and later times follow the same standard.”
Let us consider this further. Master Yan, dwelling in a humble lane, differed from Yu and Ji, who passed their doors without entering. Yet Kongzi also esteemed him as worthy, valuing his ability to judge the times. Master Yan judged the times and dwelt in a humble lane because he lacked the opportunity that Yu and Ji enjoyed. Their opportunity was to encounter Yao and Shun. That Yu and Ji encountered Yao and Shun and gained renown for their worth means that Yao and Shun brought that worth to fulfillment. Because Yao and Shun could bring the worth of Yu and Ji to fulfillment, Kongzi esteemed Yu and Ji as worthies, and Yao and Shun as sages.
Book of Changes
“Supreme good fortune in the highest position: there is great blessing.”
Huang Guohua

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
乃眷德於考成之後矣如是而不謂之大有慶
乎盖非吉不足以語慶非元吉在上不足以語
慶之大也今則行之既成即其天之已定靈承
有自克綏乎單厚之祥道之既備即其命之于
常昭鑒不違茂膺乎有秩之祜初之素履僅可
以无咎也由初以至於終則事兼美善之全而
純嘏之錫於斯爲盛矣豈惟无咎而已耶二之
履道僅得夫貞吉也視履而協於極則德會純
粹之精而休嘉之集獨享其隆矣豈惟貞吉而
===
已耶此其慎修以自淑本無徼福之心而修德
以格天自有大来之慶非爻居履之上何以得
此哉由是知天人之交其機不爽而吉凶貞勝
罔不在終君子不可以不慎也抑此聖學也惟
敬且一者能之敬則不懈一則不二是故作德
純而終始協矣天其能違之耶盖吾心之理與
天爲一心無愧怍固不必求之感應之常而即
所以得乎天也况天之助順又有不違於斯理
者哉此又視履者所當知

此哉由是知天人之交其機不爽而吉凶貞勝
罔不在終君子不可以不慎也抑此聖學也惟
敬且一者能之敬則不懈一則不二是故作德
純而終始協矣天其能違之耶蓋吾心之理與
天爲一心無愧怍固不必求之感應之常而即
所以得乎天也况天之助順又有不違於斯理
者哉此又視履者所當知
punctuated: 乃眷德於考成之後矣。如是而不謂之大有慶乎？盖非吉不足以語慶，非元吉在上不足以語慶之大也。今則行之既成，即其天之已定，靈承有自，克綏乎單厚之祥；道之既備，即其命之于常，昭鑒不違，茂膺乎有秩之祜。初之素履，僅可以无咎也；由初以至於終，則事兼美善之全，而純嘏之錫於斯爲盛矣，豈惟无咎而已耶？二之履道，僅得夫貞吉也；視履而協於極，則德會純粹之精，而休嘉之集獨享其隆矣，豈惟貞吉而已耶？此其慎修以自淑，本無徼福之心，而修德以格天，自有大来之慶。非爻居履之上，何以得此哉？由是知天人之交，其機不爽，而吉凶貞勝，罔不在終，君子不可以不慎也。抑此聖學也，惟敬且一者能之。敬則不懈，一則不二，是故作德純而終始協矣。天其能違之耶？盖吾心之理與天爲一，心無愧怍，固不必求之感應之常，而即所以得乎天也。况天之助順，又有不違於斯理者哉？此又視履者所當知。
translation_en:
…then Heaven cherishes virtue after its accomplishment has been assessed. With this being so, can it fail to be called “great cause for rejoicing”? Without good fortune, one cannot speak of rejoicing; without supreme good fortune in the uppermost position, one cannot speak of great rejoicing. Now, conduct brought to completion means that Heaven’s judgment is settled: the receipt of divine favor has its grounds, and one can rest secure in blessings of great abundance. The Way fully realized means that Heaven’s mandate abides in constancy: its luminous scrutiny finds nothing amiss, and one receives abundant, enduring blessings.

The first line’s “plain treading” can merely secure freedom from blame. Proceeding from the beginning to the end, however, one’s deeds encompass the fullness of both beauty and goodness, and the bestowal of great blessings reaches its height here. How could this be merely freedom from blame? The second line’s “treading the Way” attains only “good fortune through correctness.” But when one examines one’s treading and accords with the highest standard, one’s virtue embodies the essence of purity, and one enjoys in exceptional abundance the auspicious blessings that gather. How could this be merely good fortune through correctness?

Such a person cultivates himself carefully to improve his character, originally harboring no intention of seeking blessings. Yet by cultivating virtue and reaching Heaven, he naturally gains the joy of great blessings coming to him. How could this be attained unless the line occupied the uppermost position in Treading [Lü]? From this we know that the workings of the intercourse between Heaven and humanity do not err, and that the ultimate outcome of good and ill fortune invariably rests upon the end. The gentleman must therefore exercise care.

This, moreover, is the learning of the sages. Only those who are reverent and single-minded can achieve it. Reverence means never growing lax; single-mindedness means never being divided. Thus the practice of virtue is pure, and beginning and end accord. Could Heaven act contrary to this? The principle within our hearts is one with Heaven. If the heart is free of shame, there is certainly no need to seek confirmation in the regular workings of stimulus and response: this itself is how one gains Heaven’s favor. How much more so, then, since Heaven’s aid to those who accord with it likewise never departs from this principle! This too is something that those who examine their treading ought to know.

“One yin and one yang are called the Way. What continues it is goodness; what completes it is human nature.”
Lin Qicai

Examiner Yan, Academician, comments: “Surely the author of this essay understands the Way!”
Examiner Li, Academician, comments: “Pure and unblemished, subtle and refined.”

The Great Commentary names the movement of material force (qi) the Way; it must be through Heaven’s mandate that we perceive this. The Way resides in material force. By considering the goodness of Heaven’s mandate, we find ample evidence for human nature. What could one yin and one yang be called if not the Way? In tracing the Way to its source to show it to others, the sage means that between Heaven and earth there is fundamentally a single material force circulating: its activity and stillness are what we call yin and yang. In stillness it contains its substance and becomes yin. One yin is followed by one yang, closing and opening succeeding each other wondrously. In activity it manifests its function and becomes yang. translation_en:
…yin; contraction and expansion respond with unfathomable efficacy to what evokes them. Thus the workings of transformation have a foundation: they are not merely the spontaneous movement of a single vital force (qi). Movement and stillness are rooted in one another; this is indeed the full substance of the Way. Without this Way, the circulation of qi might almost cease. Does not the Way mean precisely the alternation of yin and yang?

Speaking of its operation in yang, there is movement succeeding stillness, constituting that which continues it. Heaven’s mandate flows forth here: the intermingling forces of creation stir the incipient workings of emergence; the Supreme Ultimate, all-embracing, operates beyond physical form and qi. Undivided and unmixed, this is called goodness. To speak of continuing goodness is to locate here the source of human nature. Goodness does not lie outside this continuation; how, then, can one say that the Way lies outside qi?

Speaking of its presence in yin, there is the bringing of each particular thing to completion, leaving nothing out, constituting that which completes it. Heaven’s mandate is bestowed here: the true essence unites wondrously and congeals at the inception of physical form; each thing’s nature and allotted destiny are set aright and become fully present as harmony is preserved and united. Wherever there is a thing, there is its governing principle: this is called nature. To speak of completing nature is to locate here the realization of goodness. Nature does not lie outside this completion; how, then, can one say that qi is not the Way?

Such is the Way’s presence in yin and yang and its manifestation in Heaven and humanity. Who could expound it without thoroughly comprehending nature and destiny? Ah! Here we see the wholeness of the Way’s substance. If the gentleman can fully realize his nature, he can resemble Heaven, and the Way finds its full expression in him. If his nature is not fully realized, he does not resemble Heaven and Earth and departs far from the Way. There is a reason why the Way is not clearly understood throughout the world. Therefore, to unite yin and yang and thereby perfect one’s virtue, one must unite movement and stillness and thereby bring one’s efforts to fruition. punctuated: 而貴乎建萬世之猷。公之營洛邑也，相宅定宅，經緯協乎時宜；而獻卜獻圖，規模極其宏遠。蓋將使我據道里之適中者爲會同之地，而敬修可願，以承休命於無疆；即陰陽之和會者爲式化之基，而祇承不怠，以迓天休之滋至。百辟享而侯於周服，天休固見於臣矣；爲之王城以朝之，庶乎位德元以正百辟，數不可得而限也。萬姓悅而附我大邑，天休固動於民矣；爲之下都以臨之，庶乎服土中以撫萬姓，曆不可得而窮也。向以基命未定，我不敢知；今則善始之中，已裕夫善終之計，而萬億年天地同其悠久，此固公之所以爲心耳。向以定命未允，我不敢必；今則可大之規，已寓夫可久之業，而萬億年宗社藉以靈長，此固公之所以爲謀耳。夫周公宅洛之意如此，而成王體之，又豈敢有怠忽哉？抑周之君臣動稽諸天，而言必本於敬者，以天人之迹遠，而敬肆之幾甚微也。遠則難通，微則易忽，而一念少殊，安危治亂基之矣。成王不曰□之
translation_en:
…but values establishing a plan for ten thousand generations. When you, Duke, laid out Luoyi, you examined and determined the site; its planning accorded with the needs of the time. You presented the divination results and the plans, and the design was exceedingly grand and far-reaching. Your intention was to have me occupy a place centrally situated in terms of travel distances as the site for assemblies of the feudal lords, and reverently cultivate what is worthy of aspiration, thereby receiving Heaven’s favorable mandate without end. You would make this place, where yin and yang meet harmoniously, the foundation for exemplary transformation, reverently upholding my charge without slackening, to welcome Heaven’s blessings in ever greater abundance. The many lords offer tribute and submit to Zhou: Heaven’s blessings are already manifest among the ministers. You built the royal city in which to receive their homage, hoping that, occupying the position of foremost virtue, I might set the many lords aright for a span beyond reckoning. The myriad people joyfully adhere to our great city: Heaven’s blessings already stir among the people. You built the secondary capital from which to govern them, hoping that, exercising authority at the center of the land, I might nurture the myriad people for years without limit.

Formerly, because the founding mandate was not yet secure, I did not dare presume to know the outcome. Now, within this good beginning, ample provision has already been made for a good ending, so that for countless millions of years our endurance may equal that of Heaven and Earth. This was surely what you, Duke, held in your heart. Formerly, because the securing of the mandate was not yet assured, I did not dare count upon it. Now, within a design capable of greatness, there already resides an undertaking capable of enduring, through which the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain may enjoy blessed longevity for countless millions of years. This was surely what you, Duke, intended in your planning.

Such was the Duke of Zhou’s intention in establishing the seat at Luo. King Cheng understood it: how could he dare be negligent? Moreover, the rulers and ministers of Zhou referred their actions to Heaven, and invariably grounded their words in reverence, because the workings of Heaven and humanity are far apart, while the incipient distinction between reverence and heedlessness is exceedingly subtle. What is distant is difficult to connect with; what is subtle is easily overlooked. Yet a slight difference in a single thought lays the foundation for security or peril, order or disorder. King Cheng did not say, “[illegible] of …” [?]

…its blessings, but insists on speaking of reverence—was this not also something he gained from the Duke of Zhou’s guidance and nurture?

“Demarcate anew the suburbs and boundaries; carefully secure the territorial defenses, so as to bring peace to all within the Four Seas.”
Zhang Fengqi

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Chief Supervising Secretary: This ably brings out the Zhou king’s intention to preserve good government. Its language is also dignified: it is among the very best interpretations of the Classics.
Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Examining Editor: Maintaining order in the eastern suburbs depended on restoring and implementing the Duke of Zhou’s established institutions. This composition grasps that point.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor: It portrays the Zhou king’s intention to check harmful developments at their inception and guard against the slightest signs of trouble so vividly that it appears before one’s eyes. Its author must be devoted to classical learning. It should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Cao, Compiler: It explains the intention to uphold the dignity of the royal domain, and its argument itself has a dignified bearing.
Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: The prose is richly refined, and the writing vigorous and assured.
Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: It captures the meaning of King Kang’s charge to the Duke of Bi.

When a worthy king gives a charge to a great minister, he wishes him to put the principal defenses in order so as to bring peace to the realm. The suburbs, boundaries, and territorial defenses constitute the principal safeguards of the royal domain. Does not the means of bringing peace to the realm lie in putting these in order as circumstances require? The meaning of King Kang’s charge to the Duke of Bi was as though he said: Those skilled in governing the people establish great policies to invigorate the transforming influence of renewal. Above all, they must give weight to the overall configuration of power when planning for the foundations of rule. Thus, under the former kings, the suburbs and boundaries had certainly already been planned and demarcated; but as the years pass, it is easy…

punctuated: 湮，將無或潰其防者乎？殆必申而畫之：遠郊近郊，截然條理之不紊；圻內圻外，秩然界限之必明。非必盡易其規，而所以圖舊以增之新者，當不遺其力焉。封域之在先王，亦有常守矣。世平易玩，將無或懈其事者乎？殆必慎而固之：捍衞遴其人，以嚴怠弛之戒；保障密其法，以峻出入之防。非必盡易其舊，而所以振廢以作其氣者，思以殫其心焉。夫是固所以飭王畿也。然郊圻申畫，則體統尊而綱維著，有以警殷民覬覦之心；封守慎固，則藩屏嚴而紀律張，有以杜遠人窺伺之念。風聲覃被，非獨在洛之見旌者有所恃而不恐，而四海式化，莫不臻康乂之休也；聲教遠訖，匪獨在洛之見別者有所畏而不為，而四海承德，莫不獲寧謐之慶也。是知奠王畿者，篤近也，其威自行于遠；康四海者，舉遠也，其端實本于近。然則洛邑根本之地，而可勿圖乎？抑考畢公四世元老，去周公未久，而洛邑郊圻封守，乃康王拳拳為言，若虞其遽廢者，何耶？蓋保
translation_en:
…become obscured: might there not be some breach in their defenses? Surely the boundaries must be demarcated anew: the outer and inner suburbs must be distinctly ordered, without confusion; the areas within and beyond the royal domain must have orderly and unmistakable boundaries. It is not necessary to change the entire arrangement, but no effort should be spared in planning on the basis of the old and supplementing it with the new. Under the former kings, the territorial boundaries likewise had established defenses. In peaceful times it is easy to grow careless: might there not be some neglect of these duties? Surely the defenses must be carefully strengthened: select the right men to guard them, enforcing strict precautions against negligence; make the regulations for their protection thorough, strengthening controls over entry and departure. It is not necessary to change all the old arrangements, but one should devote one's whole mind to restoring what has fallen into disuse and reviving its vigor.

These are indeed the means of putting the royal domain in order. Yet when the suburban boundaries are demarcated anew, the hierarchy gains dignity and the governing framework becomes manifest, thereby checking the covetous designs of the people of Yin. When the frontier defenses are carefully strengthened, the protective barriers become formidable and discipline is enforced, thereby forestalling the designs of distant peoples watching for an opportunity. The influence of royal authority spreads widely: not only do those honored in Luo have something to rely upon and thus remain free from fear, but all within the Four Seas follow its transforming example and attain the blessings of peace and good order. Its prestige and moral instruction reach far: not only do those singled out for censure in Luo have something to fear and thus refrain from wrongdoing, but all within the Four Seas receive its virtue and enjoy the blessings of tranquility.

Thus we know that securing the royal domain means strengthening what is near, while its awe-inspiring authority naturally extends afar; bringing peace to all within the Four Seas means attending to what is distant, while its starting point is truly rooted in what is near. Since Luoyi is the foundation, then, can one fail to plan for it? Consider, moreover, that the Duke of Bi was a senior statesman who had served four reigns, and that not long had passed since the Duke of Zhou. Why, then, did King Kang speak so earnestly about Luoyi's suburban boundaries and territorial defenses, as though fearing their sudden abandonment? For preserving…

…in preserving good order, what matters is to discern the first signs beforehand and examine them carefully; if one begins planning only when trouble arrives, it will be too late. The Book of Odes says: “Before the sky grows overcast and rain falls, bind fast the windows and doors.” Ah! King Kang understood this; fitting indeed was his preservation of tranquil order!

Book of Odes
“The king commanded Nan Zhong
To go and build fortifications at Fang.
The chariots went forth in great numbers;
The banners and standards were splendid.
The Son of Heaven commanded us
To fortify that northern region.
Illustrious was Nan Zhong;
The Xianyun were swept away.”
Cai Maochun

Examiner Li, Academician, comments: “He has grasped the poet’s meaning and purpose, and his powers are sufficient to express them. Hence its inclusion.”

The great commander received the charge to prepare the frontier’s defenses and thereby achieved the pacification of the frontier. Indeed, the way to resist the Rong lay simply in building fortifications and defending them. The king of Zhou charged his commander with this task, and Nan Zhong exerted himself mightily to accomplish it. Was this not why the poem celebrated him? The intent of the composer of “Bringing Out the Chariots” (Chu che) was as if to say: Shuofang is where Heaven set the boundary between the Chinese and the barbarians. By fortifying Shuofang, the king wished to repel the barbarians and bring peace to the Chinese. Thus, having Nan Zhong as a commander, the king commissioned him; to build fortifications at Shuofang, the king sent him there. In entrusting great authority to a venerable man, he obtained the right person; in strengthening the great defenses and holding strategic points, he obtained the right strategy.

As soon as Nan Zhong received this command, he brought his might into action. The instruments effective for charging and breaking through were the chariots: numerous and powerful, they advanced bearing righteousness, providing equipment of proven solidity. The means of coordinating advances and halts were the banners: splendidly displayed, they moved manifesting martial spirit, presenting a most imposing appearance. Nan Zhong wished to unite the resolve of his men and rouse their courage. Accordingly, he expressly proclaimed the king’s command and made its awe-inspiring authority felt, telling them: “The Son of Heaven has commanded me to fortify that Shuofang.”

To say that the command issued from the Son of Heaven made manifest its august source: entrusted with military command, I dare not fail in reverence and obedience. translation_en:
…must cooperate. A capable commander leads troops governed by discipline; with a reverent heart he reiterates stern commands. How awe-inspiring was this Nan Zhong! His reputation alone could overwhelm the enemy’s spirit. He first made himself invincible and then awaited an opportunity to defeat the enemy. He did not engage rashly in battle, but acted only with every assurance of success. Those who posed such an urgent threat were driven away by his awe-inspiring might, and the difficulties of the king’s service were resolved. He did not pursue warfare to exhaustion or abuse military force, but maintained defenses against the peoples of the four quarters. Those who would not yield [?] were eliminated by his awe-inspiring might, and the fulfillment of the royal command [illegible character]. Thus, to build fortifications at Shuofang, it was indeed fitting that Nan Zhong should receive the commission; and driving off the Xianyun was surely his great achievement. It was fitting, then, to reward him when the army returned. Nevertheless, Nan Zhong’s achievement was the Son of Heaven’s achievement. For fortifying Shuofang was the Son of Heaven’s intention, and it was the Son of Heaven who commissioned Nan Zhong. Thus we call it the Son of Heaven’s achievement. Moreover, the Son of Heaven employed men who were filial, brotherly, gentle, and good, who assisted him daily at his side. Nan Zhong could therefore carry out his defensive plans undisturbed, without interference from commands issued at a distance. This was what enabled him to succeed, and was especially an achievement of the Son of Heaven.

In a later age, an imperial letter under seal replied to the General of the Rear, approving the strategy he had submitted. The veteran minister then put trenches and ramparts in order, linking the encampments [?] in Huangzhong, and thereby secured a means of subduing the Qiang and achieving victory without advancing. Ah, this came close to that earlier example!

Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler, comments: “The Duke of Zhou desired King Cheng to be wholly devoted to reverent virtue; his loyal devotion was deeply earnest. This essay alone succeeds in bringing this out.”

Examiner Li, Academician, comments: “Skillful in understanding and exposition.”

A great minister exhorts his king to cultivate virtue with undivided devotion, so that the results may follow of themselves. When virtue is cultivated and blessings arrive, there is fundamentally no need to seek them externally. Yet without enduring conformity to the Mandate, how could one be wholly devoted to cultivating virtue? Such was the Duke of Zhou’s admonition to King Cheng. It was as though he said: “Our Zhou received the Mandate through your ancestor’s virtue, so you certainly must know to keep him in mind. Yet your ancestor’s virtue was a virtue of reverence. If you remember your ancestor but do not emulate his virtue, can the dynastic enterprise be preserved? 萬化之原慎修其身以懋建乎四方之極務去
其不如爾祖者以就其如爾祖者使有以遡敬
止之源斯可矣然爾祖之敬緝熈之敬也修德
而非永於配命德其可得而成乎必也自一念
而達之於百慮內焉而罔不欽也自一事而達

無間則我之配乎命者無違務有以守緝熈之
