translation_en:
…the source of all transformations; carefully cultivate your person, diligently establishing the standard for the four quarters. Strive to eliminate whatever in you falls short of your ancestor and to achieve whatever accords with him, so that you may trace reverence back to its source. Only then will this suffice. Yet your ancestor’s reverence was a reverence continually sustained and made luminous. If, in cultivating virtue, you do not enduringly accord with Heaven’s Mandate, how can your virtue be brought to completion? You must extend a single thought to your hundred deliberations, so that inwardly nothing lacks reverence; and extend a single undertaking to the myriad affairs of government, so that outwardly nothing lacks goodness. For the principle ordained by Heaven is uninterrupted; accordingly, our accord with its Mandate must admit no deviation. Strive to uphold the standard of continuous illumination. Only then will this suffice.

Thus, through according with the Mandate, virtue is cultivated, enabling you to acknowledge and extol your ancestor’s glorious achievements; and through cultivating virtue, blessings gather, naturally enabling you fully to enjoy Heaven’s favor. “Lavishing gifts upon Zhou” was how Heaven recognized your ancestor’s virtue. Now, if your virtue does not differ from your ancestor’s, Heaven will not withhold its Mandate. Your descendants will preserve it, and the officers of Zhou will rely upon it. Those blessings that cannot be obtained by mere good fortune we shall assuredly have no cause to decline. “The great Mandate was renewed” was how your ancestor received Heaven’s favor. Now, if your virtue continues his old inheritance, the Mandate’s renewal can endure. The descendants of Yin will submit ever more fully, and Yin’s eminent officers will serve ever more faithfully as subjects. Though the Mandate does not remain forever with one house, Heaven likewise will have no cause to turn away. What could this be called but seeking abundant blessings for oneself?

Viewed in terms of the distinction between Heaven and humanity, blessings are bestowed by Heaven, and one cannot speak of seeking them oneself. But considered in terms of the workings of stimulus and response, blessings are brought about by virtue, and it is permissible to speak of seeking them oneself. Yet…

translation_en:
…Then seeking blessings requires nothing other than cultivating virtue; cultivating virtue requires nothing other than following one’s ancestors. How could a succeeding king fail to understand what he must attend to? Yet this ode repeatedly examines the reasons for the gains and losses of Yin and Zhou, while the chapter “Against Idleness” (Wuyi) also treats in detail what the common people depend upon. Why do both ultimately turn to praising King Wen? By following one’s ancestors, one cultivates virtue and can appeal to Heaven; by attending to the work of securing well-being and cultivating the fields, one gives the people something to depend upon. With these means, what difficulty is there in preserving the inherited royal enterprise? Moreover, the admonition to be wary and fearful and the injunction to abide in reverence unite the two texts in a single teaching. Thus reverence is indeed the essential means of appealing to Heaven and diligently caring for the people, and it becomes especially clear that the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents complement one another.

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
詹而自治則疎矣春秋厚於待齊得無備責之
乎齊何以執鄭詹也宋同盟也而侵之齊伯主
也而不朝焉詹聽其政固宜咎之執矣春秋乃
以惡齊者何蓋以責人之心責已則盡道以愛
已之心愛人則盡仁使桓能知此則德進於王
而奚有於詹之執也耶夫何宅心弗宏惟求諸
人而不求諸已圖伯是急不示之德而遽示之
刑人之虐鄰吾所惡也而重怒之凌其何以堪
獨不可以之自反乎人之親已吾所欲也而惠
===
徼之願其孰無懷獨不可推之愛人乎使桓而
非伯也固無望焉爾伯如桓天下方賴其安者
而乃一朝之不忍果罪之在鄭耶抑罪之在齊
耶使桓而非賢也亦無責焉爾賢如桓諸侯方
望其賜者而乃一眚之不宥果鄭之不能事齊
耶抑齊之不能撫鄭耶聖人以為王者厚於責
躬故不親反仁不治反智而人無不服恕以及
物故招携以禮懷遠以德而物無不親惜也桓
公不足以語此詹之執悖於道而違於仁矣其

…Zhan, yet was remiss in governing himself. The Spring and Autumn Annals sets high expectations for Qi: could it fail to hold Qi fully accountable? Why did Qi arrest Zhan of Zheng? Song was a fellow member of the covenant, yet Zheng invaded it; Qi was the hegemonic lord, yet Zheng failed to attend its court. Zhan directed Zheng’s government, so it was surely fitting to blame and arrest him. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals make this grounds for censuring Qi? Because one fulfills the Way by holding oneself to account with the same mind with which one holds others to account, and fulfills benevolence by loving others with the same mind with which one loves oneself. Had Duke Huan understood this, his virtue would have advanced toward that of a true king. What occasion would there then have been to arrest Zhan? Why was his disposition so ungenerous, demanding things of others but not of himself, intent on securing hegemony, and hastily displaying punishment instead of virtue? We detest others’ oppression of their neighbors; if we compound it with the oppression of our own anger, how can they endure it? Could he not have turned this judgment back upon himself? We desire others’ affection; who does not harbor the wish to obtain kindness [?]? Could he not have extended this feeling to loving others?

Had Duke Huan not been hegemon, there would indeed have been no such expectations of him. But with a hegemon such as Huan, all under Heaven were relying on him for peace, and yet he could not master a moment’s anger. Did the fault truly lie with Zheng, or did it lie with Qi? Had Duke Huan not been worthy, there would likewise have been no such demands upon him. But with a worthy ruler such as Huan, the feudal lords were looking to him for favors, and yet he would not pardon a single fault. Was it truly that Zheng could not serve Qi, or that Qi could not nurture Zheng?

The Sage considered that a true king is exacting in holding himself accountable. Thus, when others do not draw close to him, he examines his own benevolence; when they are not well governed, he examines his own wisdom. Consequently, none fail to submit. He extends sympathetic understanding to others, drawing in the estranged through ritual propriety and winning over the distant through virtue; consequently, none fail to draw close. title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
何以宗諸侯哉故春秋書齊人執鄭詹以見其
不得爲伯討盖望之深故責之備也不然豈厚
於鄭而薄於齊耶抑齊桓君臣每於成功而無
以居之幽之盟諸侯服矣而詹執召陵之盟楚
人帖矣而濤塗執盖桓量淺而仲器不宏也故
君子觀于斯未嘗不嘆其志之易驕而卒無以
服楚懷鄭者有由矣噫此王道敦不息之誠而

…how could he be the leader of the feudal lords? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records, “The men of Qi seized Zhan of Zheng,” to show that this could not count as a hegemon’s punitive action. Because its expectations of him were high, its demands upon him were exacting. Otherwise, would it have been generous toward Zheng but harsh toward Qi? Moreover, Duke Huan of Qi and his ministers repeatedly achieved success but failed to sustain it. At the covenant at You, the feudal lords had submitted, yet Zhan was seized; at the covenant at Shaoling, the men of Chu had yielded, yet Taotu was seized. This was because Duke Huan lacked magnanimity and Guan Zhong’s capacity was limited. Hence gentlemen contemplating these events invariably lament how readily their ambitions turned to arrogance. There was a reason why they ultimately failed to secure Chu’s submission and win Zheng’s allegiance. Alas! This is why the Kingly Way cultivates unceasing sincerity; surely the Spring and Autumn Annals could not have treated Duke Huan otherwise!

能若是乎齊自桓公肇伯以来無日不以競詐
力為事魯為之弱久矣夾谷之會何以見化行
於齊乎盖天下莫大於理齊聽犁彌之謀以夷
謀夏以俘干盟於理悖矣我魯所以有辭也於
是孔子率古道以當其變一言而齊之君臣瞿
然以服裔夷却而三軍之衆無所用其強矣甚
哉理之足以服人也使究其效焉則王道所達
如舜之苗格文之崇降固可推之天下而準也
其感而服者豈獨一齊乎故經紀之見聖人化
===
行於外如此魯自季宿專國以来無日不以自

甲兵邑有城池於禮僭矣家隸所以為資也於

然以從私邑毀而百雉之城無以負其固矣甚

How does the meeting at Jiagu reveal the transforming influence at work in Qi? Nothing under Heaven is greater than moral principle. Qi heeded Li Mi’s scheme, using barbarians to plot against the people of the central states and captives to disrupt a covenant. This violated principle and thus gave our state of Lu grounds for remonstrance. Confucius therefore followed the ancient Way to meet this emergency. Ji acceded to Nan Yi’s request: his household possessed armor and weapons, and his town had walls and moats. title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
者之意若曰教之至者莫大於範世而德之至
者莫盛於法天何則立天之道曰陰與陽而太
極動靜之理乘焉錯行代明不已以妙其用散
殊同化相禪以神其機運之為命而默示於無
言者有以肇禮樂之本顯諸其仁而昭垂於有
象者所以開制作之原易簡廣大凡其形而上
者無非教也至精至微夫孰得而加之哉聖人
作則曰禮與樂而精神心術之蘊形焉威儀交
錯秩乎其有章小大相成純然其罔間求端於
===
天載之神而和序之妙與造化以同流效法于
於穆之運而制作之功與陰陽而合德中正和
樂凡其得於身者莫非德也盡善盡美夫孰得
而加之哉是則天道至教至德之本所以立也
聖人至德至教之用所以行也觀於此而天人
一致之妙可見矣抑論道原于天德教之所從
出也聖人體道於身而制禮作樂豈惟合德於
天而已哉所以明天道以教天下後世其贊化
育之功於是乎為大矣世之視禮樂者不究其

punctuated: 者之意若曰：教之至者，莫大於範世；而德之至者，莫盛於法天。何則？立天之道曰陰與陽，而太極動靜之理乘焉。錯行代明，不已以妙其用；散殊同化，相禪以神其機。運之為命，而默示於無言者，有以肇禮樂之本；顯諸其仁，而昭垂於有象者，所以開制作之原。易簡廣大，凡其形而上者，無非教也。至精至微，夫孰得而加之哉？聖人作則曰禮與樂，而精神心術之蘊形焉。威儀交錯，秩乎其有章；小大相成，純然其罔間。求端於天載之神，而和序之妙與造化以同流；效法于於穆之運，而制作之功與陰陽而合德。中正和樂，凡其得於身者，莫非德也。盡善盡美，夫孰得而加之哉？是則天道至教，至德之本所以立也；聖人至德，至教之用所以行也。觀於此，而天人一致之妙可見矣。抑論道原于天，德教之所從出也。聖人體道於身，而制禮作樂，豈惟合德於天而已哉？所以明天道以教天下後世，其贊化育之功，於是乎為大矣。世之視禮樂者，不究其

…the writer’s meaning seems to be this: nothing is greater in perfect teaching than setting a pattern for the world, and nothing is more exalted in perfect virtue than modeling oneself on Heaven. Why is this? What establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang, and within them operates the principle of movement and stillness of the Supreme Ultimate. They act in alternation and take turns manifesting themselves, ceaselessly displaying the subtlety of their workings. Differentiated in their manifestations yet united in transformation, they succeed one another, rendering their operation wondrous. That which moves as Heaven’s mandate and silently instructs without words establishes the foundation of rites and music. That which manifests in its benevolence and shines forth in visible forms opens the source of the creation of institutions. Easy and simple, broad and great: everything in Heaven that lies beyond physical form is teaching. Utterly refined and utterly subtle—who could surpass it?

The standards established by the sage are called rites and music; through them, the depths of his spirit and the workings of his mind take form. His dignified deportment and ceremonial observances interweave, ordered in distinct patterns; the small and the great complete one another, forming a pure and uninterrupted whole. He seeks their beginnings in the wondrous activity of Heaven, so that the subtle harmony and order they embody flow together with cosmic creation and transformation. He models himself on Heaven’s profound operation, so that his achievement in creating institutions accords in virtue with yin and yang. Centered and correct, harmonious and joyful: all that he realizes in his own person is virtue. Perfectly good and perfectly beautiful—who could surpass it?

Thus, the Way of Heaven is perfect teaching, whereby the foundation of perfect virtue is established; the sage’s perfect virtue is that whereby the operation of perfect teaching is put into practice. From this, one can perceive the subtle unity of Heaven and humanity. Further, to discuss the matter: the Way originates in Heaven, the source from which virtue and teaching issue. When the sage embodies the Way in his person and institutes rites and creates music, does he merely accord in virtue with Heaven? Through these he elucidates the Way of Heaven to teach the world and later generations. Herein lies the greatness of his achievement in assisting cosmic transformation and nurture. punctuated:
制作之原，乃曰器數之末，而道不在是。噫！是豈足以知聖人之於天道哉？

凡音者，生人心者也。情動於中，故形於聲；聲成文，謂之音。是故治世之音安以樂，其政和。

張憲臣

同考試官署員外郎王批：辭瑩義精，鏗然可誦，亦可謂治世之文者。

同考試官侍讀胡批：發慎感意，明淨。

考試官學士嚴批：即謂之聲成文者，非耶？

考試官學士李批：是文生於心者，可錄。

記者原音本於心而和於政，見感之當慎也。蓋心以政感，音之所自生也；政和則音和矣。此先王之所以慎感乎！今夫人心之所因以宣者，音也；而其所由以動者，感也。感之於人大矣哉！何則？樂由音以生，夫豈無所自耶？蓋人之有心，其渾然在中者，涵聲氣之元，而音之本則在是焉；寂然不動者，具感通之妙，而音之用所由生焉。
translation_en:
…the origins of their creation, yet say that these are merely the minutiae of implements and numerical prescriptions, and that the Way does not reside in them. Alas! How could this suffice to understand the sage’s relationship to the Way of Heaven?

“All musical tones arise from the human heart. Feelings stir within and thus take form in sounds; when sounds form patterns, they are called musical tones. Thus the music of a well-governed age is tranquil and joyful, for its government is harmonious.”

Zhang Xianchen

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Acting Vice Director: “The wording is polished and the meaning refined; it rings out when recited. This, too, may be called the writing of a well-governed age.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Hu, Reader-in-waiting: “It develops the idea of exercising care over what moves the heart, clearly and cleanly.”

Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: “This is precisely what is meant by sounds forming patterns, is it not?”

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: “This writing arises from the heart; it merits inclusion.”

The recorder traces musical tones to their root in the heart and their harmony to government, showing that care must be taken over the influences that move the heart. For the heart is moved by government, and this is where musical tones originate; when government is harmonious, the tones are harmonious as well. Surely this is why the former kings exercised care over such influences! Now, musical tones are the means through which the human heart finds expression, while external influences are what set it in motion. How great is the importance of these influences for human beings! Why is this so? Music arises from musical tones; could these possibly have no source? Within the human heart, its undivided wholeness contains the primal source of sound and vital energy: here lies the root of musical tones. In its stillness, before it is stirred, it possesses the wondrous capacity to respond and communicate: from this arises the functioning of musical tones. …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
物感而動喜怒哀樂之情則永言以宣之不容
以自己也有弗形於聲乎聲應而生清濁高下
之變則依永以比之由是以成文也斯不謂之
音乎夫音之生本於心之感而觀其所感則上
之政爲之是故至治之世形之歌咏以揚其自
得之休者安舒而不迫發於聲音以鳴夫太平
之盛者懽樂而不流音之至和也審音而政可
知矣其禮序樂和而德教溢焉政均刑措而王
道備焉故政善則民安樂心由之以感也心和
===
則氣和和聲於是乎生也政之與音其爲感通
之本豈不大哉先王慎其所以感之蓋知本矣
雖然君心出政之本也古昔聖人以純王之心
發而爲純王之政故能以感人心之和而音生
焉由是作樂以宣暢其和而天地官萬物育者
胥此矣苟無聖人之心而欲求其政之和以感
人烏可得哉故曰聖人感人心而天下和平
第貳場
論

punctuated:
物感而動，喜怒哀樂之情，則永言以宣之，不容以自己也，有弗形於聲乎？聲應而生，清濁高下之變，則依永以比之，由是以成文也，斯不謂之音乎？夫音之生，本於心之感，而觀其所感，則上之政爲之。是故至治之世，形之歌咏以揚其自得之休者，安舒而不迫；發於聲音以鳴夫太平之盛者，懽樂而不流，音之至和也。審音而政可知矣。其禮序樂和而德教溢焉，政均刑措而王道備焉。故政善則民安樂，心由之以感也；心和則氣和，和聲於是乎生也。政之與音，其爲感通之本，豈不大哉？先王慎其所以感之，蓋知本矣。雖然，君心出政之本也。古昔聖人以純王之心，發而爲純王之政，故能以感人心之和而音生焉。由是作樂以宣暢其和，而天地官、萬物育者，胥此矣。苟無聖人之心，而欲求其政之和以感人，烏可得哉？故曰：「聖人感人心而天下和平。」

第貳場

論
translation_en:
…When external things stir the heart into motion, the feelings of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure are expressed in prolonged utterance and cannot be restrained. Could they fail to take shape in sound? Sounds arise in response; their variations in clarity and turbidity, pitch high and low, are arranged according to the prolonged utterance, thereby forming patterns. Is this not what is called musical tone? The production of musical tone is rooted in the heart’s being moved; and if we examine what moves it, we find that it is the government of those above. Thus, in an age of perfect government, songs that express the beauty of people’s contentment are relaxed and unhurried; sounds that proclaim the flourishing of great peace are joyful without excess. This is musical tone at its most harmonious. By examining musical tones, one can know the character of government. Ritual brings order and music brings harmony, while moral instruction abounds; government is equitable and punishments are set aside, while the Kingly Way is fully realized. Thus, when government is good, the people are peaceful and happy, and their hearts are moved accordingly. When their hearts are harmonious, their vital energies are harmonious, and harmonious sounds arise from this. How great is the role of government as the foundation of the sympathetic connection between government and musical tone! The former kings were cautious about how they moved people’s hearts: they understood the root.

Yet the ruler’s heart is the root from which government issues. The sages of antiquity brought forth government wholly consonant with true kingship from hearts wholly devoted to true kingship. Thus they could evoke harmony in people’s hearts, from which musical tones arose. They then made music to express and give free course to this harmony. That Heaven and Earth are properly ordered [?] and the myriad things are nurtured all derives from this. Without the heart of a sage, how could one hope to attain harmony in government and thereby move others? Thus it is said: “The sage moves people’s hearts, and all under Heaven becomes peaceful and harmonious.”

考試官學士嚴　批格如陳㵎如蘇氣如歐
考試官學士李　批認理親切措詞昌達
===
聖人坊天下以禮而實教天下以心是故因諸
情以爲之本詳諸制以爲之文协諸中以爲之
極性具而中涵焉禮制而中形焉此其合一之
妙固有不待聖人而各自足者然而猶不一者
punctuated:
聖人所以合内外之道
蔡茂春

同考試官郎中王批：典實純正，發明聖人制禮之意，親切有味，可以觀其素養矣。
同考試官都給事中藍批：格髙而詞古，氣昌而思精，開闔變化而卒澤於理，是真達禮之本者。佳士！佳士！
同考試官編修趙批：理正詞雅，氣宏意暢，而條理燦然，是必能履仁迪義而自檢以禮者。
同考試官編修王批：洞究聖人制禮本原，而純粹之學、博雅之才，又足以發之，真經緯之文也。
同考試官編修季批：仁義禮本自一貫，此篇根極要領，發揮精到，宜錄之以示窮理之學。
考試官學士嚴批：格如陳，瀾如蘇，氣如歐。
考試官學士李批：認理親切，措詞昌達。

聖人坊天下以禮，而實教天下以心。是故因諸性以為之本，詳諸制以為之文，協諸中以為之極。性具而中涵焉，禮制而中形焉。此其合一之妙，固有不待聖人而各自足者。然而情不一者
translation_en:
The Way by Which the Sage Unites the Inner and the Outer
Cai Maochun

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler: Its principles are correct, its diction elegant, its spirit expansive, and its meaning freely expressed, while its orderly reasoning shines forth. This must be someone capable of practicing benevolence, following righteousness, and regulating himself through ritual.

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
或失則渙分不一者或失則乖而民之心日遠
於中矣聖人知夫是不可長也制為之禮以坊
之而其所為禮則亦取諸人心仁義之性節而
文之以遂其所欲致夫是以天下之人便其法
制之詳可因以自守而又内悟於心安其立教
之非強相率從之由其理以得其性而化中之
治卒以大成於天下然則聖人因性制禮而實
先之於其内天下因禮悟性而常得之於其外
夫固以其心之一者相通耳不然則私智所成
===
民悖弗信又何以立教而建之極哉故曰聖人
所以合内外之道吾獨怪夫後之論者岐而二
之而使聖人制禮之原不白也彼其是内而非
外者則曰禮者忠信之薄曰聖人滅性起偽而
不知心者文之隱内者未始不外也使内而無
與於其外則其内為枯寂而非所以謂之性矣
徇外而遺内者則曰聖人制禮有術焉輕去其
故而不知文者心之著外者未始不内也使外
而無與於其内則其外為贅疣而非所以謂之

於中矣聖人知夫是不可長也制為之禮以坊

文之以遂其所欲致夫是以天下之人便其法
制之詳可因以自守而又內悟於心安其立教
之非強相率從之由其理以得其性而化中之
治卒以大成於天下然則聖人因性制禮而實
先之於其內天下因禮悟性而常得之於其外
夫固以其心之一者相通耳不然則私智所感
===
民悖弗信又何以立教而建之極哉故曰聖人
所以合內外之道吾獨怪夫後之論者岐而二
之而使聖人制禮之原不白也彼其是內而非
外者則曰禮者忠信之薄曰聖人滅性起偽而
不知心者文之隱內者未始不外也使內而無
與於其外則其內為枯寂而非所以謂之性矣
狥外而遺內者則曰聖人制禮有術焉輕去其
故而不知文者心之著外者未始不內也使外
而無與於其內則其外為贅疣而非所以謂之
punctuated:
或失則渙，分不一者或失則乖，而民之心日遠於中矣。聖人知夫是不可長也，制為之禮以坊之，而其所為禮，則亦取諸人心仁義之性，節而文之，以遂其所欲致夫。是以天下之人便其法制之詳，可因以自守，而又内悟於心，安其立教之非強，相率從之，由其理以得其性，而化中之治卒以大成於天下。然則聖人因性制禮，而實先之於其内；天下因禮悟性，而常得之於其外。夫固以其心之一者相通耳。不然，則私智所成，民悖弗信，又何以立教而建之極哉？故曰：「聖人所以合内外之道。」
吾獨怪夫後之論者岐而二之，而使聖人制禮之原不白也。彼其是内而非外者，則曰：「禮者忠信之薄。」曰：「聖人滅性起偽。」而不知心者文之隱，内者未始不外也。使内而無與於其外，則其内為枯寂，而非所以謂之性矣。徇外而遺内者，則曰：「聖人制禮有術焉。」輕去其故，而不知文者心之著，外者未始不内也。使外而無與於其内，則其外為贅疣，而非所以謂之
translation_en:
…when they go astray, they become dispersed; where allotted stations differ, going astray brings discord, and the people’s hearts grow daily more distant from the Mean. Knowing that this could not be allowed to continue, the sages instituted ritual to restrain them. The ritual they devised likewise drew upon the benevolence and righteousness inherent in human hearts, regulating these and giving them patterned expression, so as to fulfill what people wished to attain [?]. Thus people throughout the realm found the detailed regulations convenient and could rely on them to govern their own conduct. They also gained inward understanding in their hearts, finding assurance that the teachings established by the sages were not imposed by force. They followed one another in adhering to them, following their principles to realize their own nature. Government that transformed people through the Mean [?] was thereby fully accomplished throughout the realm. Thus the sages instituted ritual on the basis of human nature, but in truth began with what was within; people throughout the realm awakened to their nature through ritual, but consistently attained it through what was without. They were indeed connected through the unity of their hearts. Otherwise, if ritual were the product of private ingenuity, the people would resist it and withhold their trust: how then could teachings be established and an ultimate standard set up? Hence the saying: “This is the way by which the sages unite the inner and the outer.”
What puzzles me is that later commentators divided these into two, obscuring the source from which the sages instituted ritual. Those who affirm the inner and reject the outer say, “Ritual is the attenuation of loyalty and trustworthiness,” and, “The sages extinguish human nature and bring forth artifice.” They do not understand that the heart is the hidden aspect of patterned expression, and that the inner has never been separate from the outer. If the inner had no connection with the outer, it would be barren stillness, not what we call human nature. Those who pursue the outer and neglect the inner say, “The sages had techniques for instituting ritual.” They lightly discard its underlying reasons, failing to understand that patterned expression is the manifestation of the heart, and that the outer has never been separate from the inner. If the outer had no connection with the inner, it would be a useless excrescence, not what we call…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
文矣今夫天高地下萬物散殊而禮制行焉記
禮者嘗有是言矣然究而言之孰高下是孰散
殊是沖漠無朕之中而萬象森然已具則內外
之合在天地亦莫不然者何獨至聖人而疑之
吾嘗觀之人於身有耳目口體而其接於人有
所謂君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友之五者其耳目
口體必有視聽言動之用其接於君臣父子夫
婦長幼朋友必有事以成其倫是禮文之所由
生也至其觸於外而驗之心則吾見其固有藹
===
然而相親者矣固有粲然而相讓者矣是則仁
義之實而禮之本也是心也見於耳目口體則
為視聽言動之中見於君臣父子夫婦長幼朋
友則為親義序別信之中茲所謂內外合一之
原而夫人與聖人者一也苟其善推而不窮則
其隆殺曲直莫不各有天然之則又何俟於聖
人之禮乎惟夫好惡無節於內知誘於外而其
所謂中者斯梏之亡矣雖其間資稟稍厚或時
率其愛求以達乎心之仁而怡愉子惠漫無差

爲視聽言動之中見於君臣父子夫婦長幼朋
===
友則爲親義序別信之中茲所謂內外合一之

其隆殺曲直莫不各有天然之則又何俟於聖
人之禮乎惟夫好惡無節於內知誘於外而其
所謂中者斯梏之亡矣雖其間資禀稍厚或時
率其愛求以達乎心之仁而怡愉子惠漫無差
punctuated:
文矣。今夫天高地下，萬物散殊，而禮制行焉。記禮者嘗有是言矣。然究而言之，孰高下是？孰散殊是？沖漠無朕之中，而萬象森然已具，則內外之合，在天地亦莫不然者，何獨至聖人而疑之？
吾嘗觀之，人於身有耳目口體，而其接於人，有所謂君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友之五者。其耳目口體必有視聽言動之用，其接於君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友，必有事以成其倫，是禮文之所由生也。至其觸於外而驗之心，則吾見其固有藹然而相親者矣，固有粲然而相讓者矣。是則仁義之實，而禮之本也。是心也，見於耳目口體，則為視聽言動之中；見於君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友，則為親義序別信之中。茲所謂內外合一之原，而夫人與聖人者一也。苟其善推而不窮，則其隆殺曲直，莫不各有天然之則，又何俟於聖人之禮乎？惟夫好惡無節於內，知誘於外，而其所謂中者，斯梏之亡矣。雖其間資稟稍厚，或時率其愛，求以達乎心之仁，而怡愉子惠，漫無差
translation_en:
…outward form. Now, Heaven is high and Earth low; the myriad things are dispersed and differentiated, and ritual order operates among them. Those who recorded the rites once spoke thus. Yet, examining the matter fully, what makes these high and low? What disperses and differentiates them? Within the silent emptiness where no trace is yet apparent, the myriad forms are already fully arrayed. Thus the union of inner and outer holds throughout Heaven and Earth. Why doubt it only when we come to the sages?
I have observed that people possess ears, eyes, mouths, and bodies, and that their dealings with others involve the five relationships called ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend. Their ears, eyes, mouths, and bodies necessarily serve the functions of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting; their dealings within these five relationships necessarily involve acts through which those relationships are fulfilled. This is how ritual forms arise. When people encounter things outside themselves and examine their hearts, I see that they inherently possess a warm affection for one another and a manifest disposition to yield to one another. These are the substance of benevolence and righteousness, and the foundation of ritual. When this heart manifests itself through ears, eyes, mouth, and body, it becomes due measure in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. When it manifests itself within the relationships of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friends, it becomes due measure in affection, righteousness, precedence, distinction, and trustworthiness. This is what is called the source of the unity of inner and outer, and in this ordinary people and sages are alike. If people could skillfully extend it without limit, then every gradation of elaboration and reduction, bending and straightening, would have its own natural rule. What further need would there be to await the sages’ rites? Yet likes and dislikes become unrestrained within, while the understanding is enticed by external things, and what is called due measure is thereby fettered and lost. Even among those whose native endowments are somewhat richer, some may at times follow their affection, seeking thereby to give full expression to the benevolence of the heart; yet their genial kindness and nurturing generosity spread without any distinction…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
等則其情之用也渙或時率其宜求以達吾心
之義而羣分縷析漠無浹洽則其分之別也乖
乖則病仁難與語義渙則病義難與語仁仁義
兩病難與語禮是性本同而交相廢矣嗚呼內
之喪而外斯悖焉外之悖而內益喪焉其勢不
至於交賊而大潰者不已矣聖人以為禮之於
民也猶坊止水所自來也坊不設則有水患而
民心罔中吾既不能使頓悟乃又無禮以坊之
則民將益便其情而莫之禁止其過豈專於民
===
哉然議禮自我不出於性而非其天然自有之
中則違於心即疑於行通於此將塞於彼又何
以強其必行於天下於是思以統一其渙而整
齊其乖也則為之辨儀物秩名位綢繆其節度
使其致謹於耳目口體之間而相習於君臣父
子夫婦長幼朋友之際者甚修而綦隆而其所
以辨所以秩所以為之綢繆者又皆本吾仁義
以為之節文而一毫私智不與焉是故吉凶軍
賓嘉冠婚喪祭別之目而周旋進退各有其度

則民將益便其情而莫之禁止其過豈𠕋於民
民心罔中吾既不能使頓悟乃又無禮以坊之
民也猶坊止水所自來也坊不設則有不患而
至於交賊而大潰者不已矣聖人以爲禮之於
之喪而外斯悖焉外之悖而内益喪焉其勢不

之義而羣分縷析漠無浹洽則其分之別也乖
等則其情之用也渙或時率其宜求以達其
===
賓嘉冠婚喪祭別之目而周旋進退各有其度
以爲之節文而一毫私智不與焉是故吉凶軍
以辨所以秩所以爲之綱繆者又皆本吾仁義
子夫婦長幼朋友之際者甚修而綦隆而其所
使其致謹於耳目口體之間而相習於君臣父
齊其乖也則爲之辨儀物秩名位綱繆其節度
以強其必行於天下於是思以統一其渙而整
中則違於心即疑於行通於此將塞於彼又何
哉然議禮自我不出於性而非其天然自有之
punctuated:
等，則其情之用也渙；或時率其宜，求以達吾心之義，而羣分縷析，漠無浹洽，則其分之別也乖。乖則病仁，難與語義；渙則病義，難與語仁。仁義兩病，難與語禮。是性本同，而交相廢矣。嗚呼！內之喪，而外斯悖焉；外之悖，而內益喪焉。其勢不至於交賊而大潰者不已矣。聖人以為禮之於民也，猶坊止水所自來也。坊不設，則有水患。而民心罔中，吾既不能使頓悟，乃又無禮以坊之，則民將益便其情，而莫之禁止，其過豈專於民哉？
然議禮自我，不出於性，而非其天然自有之中，則違於心，即疑於行；通於此，將塞於彼，又何以強其必行於天下？於是思以統一其渙，而整齊其乖也，則為之辨儀物，秩名位，綢繆其節度，使其致謹於耳目口體之間，而相習於君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友之際者，甚修而綦隆。而其所以辨、所以秩、所以為之綢繆者，又皆本吾仁義，以為之節文，而一毫私智不與焉。是故吉凶軍賓嘉、冠婚喪祭，別之目，而周旋進退各有其度
translation_en:
…distinctions of degree, then the operation of their feelings becomes diffuse. At other times, they follow what is fitting, seeking thereby to realize the righteousness of their own hearts; yet they divide things into groups and analyze every thread, coldly lacking any mutual accord, so that their distinctions become discordant. Discord impairs benevolence, making it difficult to speak with them of righteousness; diffuseness impairs righteousness, making it difficult to speak with them of benevolence. When both benevolence and righteousness are impaired, it is difficult to speak with them of ritual propriety. Thus, although these share the same root in human nature, they undermine one another. Alas! When what is within is lost, outward conduct becomes perverse; when outward conduct becomes perverse, what is within suffers still greater loss. This tendency will not cease until the two injure one another and collapse utterly. The sage considers ritual propriety among the people to be like a dike checking water where it comes flowing in. Without dikes, there will be flooding. When the people's hearts lack the mean, if I cannot bring them to sudden understanding and also provide no ritual propriety to restrain them, they will increasingly indulge their feelings, with nothing to check or forbid them. Can the fault lie entirely with the people?
Yet if, in deliberating upon ritual propriety, I proceed from myself without grounding it in human nature and its inherent, natural mean, it will conflict with the heart and thus occasion doubt in practice. What works here will meet obstruction there. How, then, could I compel its universal observance throughout the realm? Accordingly, seeking to unify what is diffuse and bring order to what is discordant, the sage distinguishes ceremonial forms and objects, orders titles and ranks, and carefully arranges their measures and limits. He thereby ensures that people's care in matters of hearing, sight, speech, and bodily conduct, and their habitual dealings between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friends, are thoroughly cultivated and brought to the highest refinement. Moreover, the principles by which he makes these distinctions, establishes this ordering, and carefully arranges these details are all rooted in his own benevolence and righteousness, which give them their measured forms; not the slightest private cleverness enters into them. Thus the auspicious, mourning, military, guest, and celebratory rites, and the rites of capping, marriage, funerals, and sacrifice, are distinguished into categories, while turning, advancing, and withdrawing each have their prescribed measure…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
也輿馬宫室旂常冕服通之意而尊卑貴賤各
有其差也縞妆端緷韠紳綦幅舄之飾而裼襲
委垂各有其宜也琮璜琚瑀齊夏和鸞定之節
而步趨疾徐各有其則也尊罍簠簋羔鴈幣篚
列之器而酳酢周折各有其方也用之有不可
易之物而非是則不安於已行之有不可亂之
數而反是則不恊於人其主於心謂之中通於
命謂之性其出吾心性者行之於禮文其行乎
禮文者原之於心性其合乎心性禮文者措之
===
於身而達之人倫聖人之所以宰制萬物而役
使羣衆者豈人力也哉故人見其仁足以長人
義足以公利以為聖人之內之善也不知此則
無體之禮而外者涵矣人見其聯之有愛辨之

translation_en:
… With carriages and horses, palaces and chambers, banners and ceremonial caps and robes, their underlying significance is made coherent, while distinctions between the exalted and the lowly, the noble and the humble, each have their proper gradations. With adornments of white silk, ceremonial garments [?], knee coverings, broad sashes, bindings, leggings, and ceremonial shoes [?], exposing or covering the upper garment, and letting its parts hang or trail, each have their proper manner. With cong and huang jade objects, ju and yu jade pendants, the Qi and Xia music, and carriage bells, their rhythms are fixed, so that walking or hastening, moving quickly or slowly, each have their rule. With wine vessels and jars, grain vessels, lambs and wild geese, silks and baskets, their implements are arrayed, so that drinking after a meal, returning a toast, and turning in ceremonial movements each have their prescribed method. In their use there are objects that cannot be substituted: without these, one is ill at ease within oneself. In their performance there are prescribed measures that cannot be confused: to contravene these is to fall out of accord with others.

What presides within the heart is called equilibrium; what connects with Heaven’s mandate is called human nature. What issues from our heart and nature is put into practice in ritual forms; what is practiced in ritual forms is traced to its source in the heart and nature. What accords with the heart, nature, and ritual forms is applied to oneself and extended to human relationships. Could the means by which the sage governs all things and directs the multitude be merely human effort?

Thus people see that his benevolence suffices to lead others and his righteousness suffices to make benefits equitable, and regard these as the sage’s inward excellence. They do not understand that these are ritual without bodily form, already embracing what is outward. People see affection in the bonds he establishes and propriety in the distinctions he makes, and regard these as the sage’s outward excellence. They do not understand that these are the substance of benevolence and righteousness, through which what is inward takes form. People see that, when he follows ritual in expressing feelings, benevolence does not become dispersed, and that, when he follows ritual in applying distinctions, righteousness does not become discordant; they regard this as the sage’s combined inward and outward excellence. They do not understand that he apprehends nature through the heart, puts equilibrium into operation through nature, and establishes ordering institutions through equilibrium: this too is inward, with no outward realm to speak of. Thus, when ritual is practiced in one’s person, vision becomes clear and hearing …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
聰言從貌恭是外之中也而莫非其心之仁義
也禮行於倫則以正君臣以篤父子以和夫婦
以睦長幼以厚朋友是外之中也而莫非其心
之仁義也禮行於天下則萬物以昌江河以流
日月以明四時以序星辰以行天地以合是外
之中也而亦莫非心之仁義也故過者則俯而
就焉曰如是而心盡聖人之禮吾不可過也其
不及者則企而及焉曰如是而後心可盡聖人
之禮吾不可以不及也其日用而不知者雖未
===
可概責其著察而相與服習其教將亦戢其無
忌憚之爲而得以寡過嗚呼豈獨當世域之而
域焉後有作者亦俟之不惑蓋立隆以爲極而
萬世莫之能損益矣何也心也性也中也推之
古今無不準者也然則聖人非能以禮取必於
人而心之性一天下後世固莫之外矣天下後
世非以其私強附於聖人而性之中一人自莫
之或違矣甞讀易至履君子辨上下定民志其
禮則嚴矣吾以爲彼徒象於天澤以成於外者

禮則嚴矣吾以爲彼徒象於天澤以成於外者
punctuated:
聰，言從，貌恭，是外之中也，而莫非其心之仁義也。禮行於倫，則以正君臣，以篤父子，以和夫婦，以睦長幼，以厚朋友，是外之中也，而莫非其心之仁義也。禮行於天下，則萬物以昌，江河以流，日月以明，四時以序，星辰以行，天地以合，是外之中也，而亦莫非心之仁義也。故過者則俯而就焉，曰：「如是而心盡，聖人之禮吾不可過也。」其不及者則企而及焉，曰：「如是而後心可盡，聖人之禮吾不可以不及也。」其日用而不知者，雖未可概責其著察，而相與服習其教，將亦戢其無忌憚之爲，而得以寡過。嗚呼！豈獨當世域之而域焉？後有作者，亦俟之不惑。蓋立隆以爲極，而萬世莫之能損益矣。何也？心也，性也，中也，推之古今無不準者也。然則聖人非能以禮取必於人，而心之性一，天下後世固莫之外矣。天下後世非以其私強附於聖人，而性之中一，人自莫之或違矣。
甞讀《易》，至《履》「君子辨上下，定民志」，其禮則嚴矣。吾以爲彼徒象於天澤以成於外者
translation_en:
…hearing is keen, speech is compliant, and demeanor is respectful. This is due measure in outward conduct, yet none of it is other than the benevolence and righteousness of the heart. When ritual is practiced in human relationships, it sets right the relationship between ruler and minister, deepens affection between father and son, brings harmony between husband and wife, fosters concord between elder and younger, and strengthens friendship. This is due measure in outward conduct, yet none of it is other than the benevolence and righteousness of the heart. When ritual is practiced throughout the world, the myriad things flourish, rivers flow, sun and moon shine, the four seasons follow their order, the stars pursue their courses, and Heaven and Earth unite. This is due measure in outward things, yet again none of it is other than the benevolence and righteousness of the heart.
Thus those who go too far lower themselves to conform to it, saying: “In this way the heart is fully realized; I must not exceed the ritual of the sage.” Those who fall short stretch upward to reach it, saying: “Only in this way can the heart be fully realized; I must not fall short of the ritual of the sage.” As for those who use it daily without knowing it, although we cannot demand of them all that they clearly understand and discern it, by collectively practicing and becoming accustomed to its teachings they will also restrain their unbridled conduct and thereby lessen their faults. Ah! Does it merely set bounds for the present age, within which people remain? Should a sage arise in a later age, it can await him without misgiving. For the highest standard has been established as the ultimate norm, and through ten thousand generations no one can subtract from or add to it. Why is this? Heart, nature, and due measure: applied to past and present, these never fail as standards. Thus it is not that the sage can use ritual to insist upon compliance from others; rather, the nature of the heart is one, and the whole world and later generations necessarily lie within it. Nor do the people of the world and later generations force themselves, for private purposes, to adhere to the sage; rather, the due measure of human nature is one, and naturally no one departs from it.
I once read the Book of Changes and came to the passage in the hexagram Treading (Lü): “The gentleman distinguishes those above from those below and settles the intentions of the people.” Its ritual order is indeed strict. I thought that this merely took Heaven and the lake as its images to bring about an outward order…

然也。及觀伯夷典禮之訓、臯陶惇典之謨，乃又喟然嘆曰：「嗟乎！寅清然後禮可典，而曰叙曰秩，必歸之天焉。信乎禮合於性而不可二也！」故善言聖人之禮之外，莫如《易》；善言聖人之禮之内，莫如《書》。合《易》與《書》，而聖人内外合者見矣。世之言禮者，吾惑焉：舍其内而弗求，日以聚訟於其外，而卒使聖人合一之禮不明於天下。曽不知性不可變，而其外有時焉。協之於心而協，則禮雖先王未之有者，猶可義起也。不然，即盡取先王之禮行之，亦祗見其信不由衷，而况併其外而失之也！善乎歐陽子有言：「三代而上，治出於一，禮樂達於天下；三代而下，治出於二，禮樂爲虚文。」嗚呼！其有所見也夫！其亦有所感也夫！

translation_en:
…was so. But when I examined the instruction to Bo Yi to preside over ritual and Gao Yao’s counsel to uphold the established norms, I sighed deeply and said: “Ah! Only through reverence and purity can one preside over ritual; and when speaking of its ordering and ranking, one must attribute these to Heaven. Truly, ritual accords with human nature, and the two cannot be separated!” Thus, nothing explains the outward aspects of the sages’ ritual better than the Book of Changes, and nothing explains its inward aspects better than the Book of Documents. Read the Changes and the Documents together, and the sages’ unification of the inward and outward becomes apparent.

I am perplexed by those in our age who discuss ritual. They abandon its inward aspects without investigating them and dispute its outward aspects day after day, ultimately preventing the sages’ unified ritual from being understood throughout the world. They fail to recognize that human nature cannot change, whereas its outward forms have their appropriate times. If a practice is measured against the heart and accords with it, then even a ritual unknown to the former kings may be instituted on grounds of righteousness. Otherwise, even if one adopted and performed all the former kings’ rites, this would merely reveal that one’s professions of sincerity did not come from within. How much worse if one also lost their outward forms!

Well did Master Ouyang say: “In the Three Dynasties and earlier, governance issued from a single source, and ritual and music prevailed throughout the world. After the Three Dynasties, governance issued from two sources, and ritual and music became empty forms.” Ah! Surely he had perceived something! Surely he also felt something deeply!

…resonant lingering tones, like the music of the Greater Odes, prompting three sighs of admiration for each singing: truly extraordinary!

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Chief Supervising Secretary: Its manner is dignified and orderly, its sounds ringing and resonant. Moreover, every word is exact and every sentence elegant and beautiful. This is truly beyond the reach of ordinary talent.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Senior Compiler: Its conception is subtle and profound, its diction richly beautiful, its form grand and rounded, and its spirit and cadence balanced and harmonious. This is a work that will win renown in its age.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Expositor: Its literary ornament is luxuriant, its sound ringing and clear. From its mastery of four- and six-character parallel prose, one can also discern the learning and ability stored within its author.

Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: It shines brilliantly with the radiance of the Kui and Bi constellations, patrons of literature.

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: Classical and properly formed, beautifully balanced in parallel phrases, with ringing rhythms.

On the night of the twenty-first day of the twelfth month, in winter of the fifth year of Xuande [1430], the auspicious star Hanyu appeared. Its prognostication signifies that the people are harmonious and contented and that the Yi and Di peoples submit to civilizing influence. Your servant Shiqi, holding the requisite offices, has already led the assembled officials in offering congratulations at court. Now, reverently receiving the gift of an imperial letter bearing Your Majesty’s seal, I respectfully present a poem to renew my congratulations.

I humbly reflect: In the starry heavens a radiant celestial sign appears; this supreme auspice manifests the token of a ruler who possesses the Way…

璘璣凝鸞吉兆啓無疆之曆萬國之懽聲雷動
九重之德諭
天數仰
懋敬以緝熙蓍靈承乎
帝祉敢摛詞而揚厲賡潤色乎
皇猷臣誠忻誠忭稽首頓首竊惟大君與天地
同流隨感輒應聖人以日星爲紀亦占有
孚是以德隆則晷星神理夙筌於符牒志
壹則動氣曜靈毋鏡於先幾雲旻攝提實
===
鼎契軒轅之策景明翼軫玉繩流河漘之
圖若連貝若連珠總彰政舉或聚房或聚
井竟驗邦興蓋圓轂秉陽臨鑒之明罔漏
而渾儀測緯類從之應靡愆煌煌耀青竹
之編歷歷顯白榆之種睠茲含譽摽厥瑞
輪白如玉而黃如金品高格澤大比丸而
芒比彗義掃攙槍開輝宋代以稱奇直俟
明時而表治茲蓋恭遇
皇帝陛下
punctuated:
黼座凝釐，吉兆啓無疆之曆；萬國之懽聲雷動，九重之德諭天敷。仰懋敬以緝煕，善靈承乎帝祉。敢摛詞而揚厲，庸潤色乎皇猷。臣誠忻誠忭，稽首頓首。
竊惟大君與天地同流，隨感輒應；聖人以日星為紀，未占有孚。是以德隆則晷星，神理夙筌於往牒；志壹則動氣，曜靈每鏡於先幾。雲晃攝提，寶鼎契軒轅之策；景明翼軫，玉繩流河渚之圖。若連貝，若連珠，總彰政舉；或聚房，或聚井，竟驗邦興。盖圓載秉陽，臨鑒之明罔漏；而渾儀測緯，類從之應靡慆。煌煌耀青竹之編，歴歴顯白榆之種。眷兹含譽，標厥瑞輪。白如玉而黄如金，品高格澤；大比丸而芒比彗，義掃攙搶。間輝宋代以稱竒，直俟明時而表治。兹盖恭遇皇帝陛下，
translation_en:
…Blessings gather upon the embroidered throne, and auspicious portents inaugurate a reign without limit. The joyful cries of the myriad realms resound like thunder; proclamations of imperial virtue spread across the heavens. We look up to your diligent reverence, which sustains and brightens your virtue, and to the auspicious powers that receive the blessings of the Lord on High. I venture to unfold my words in exalted praise, thereby lending lustre to the imperial designs. Your servant, truly joyful and truly delighted, bows his head and knocks it upon the ground.
I humbly reflect that the great sovereign moves in the same course as Heaven and Earth: whenever he exerts an influence, a response follows. The sage takes the sun and stars as his standards; their testimony is assured even before divination. Thus, when virtue flourishes, the sun’s shadow and the stars respond [?]; this divine principle was long ago captured in earlier records. When the will is single, it moves the vital energies, and the heavenly luminaries constantly mirror events at their earliest stirrings. Clouds shone at Sheti, and a precious tripod accorded with Xuanyuan’s calculations; radiance illuminated Yi and Zhen, and Yusheng transmitted a chart at the river islet [?]. Whether like linked cowries or strung pearls, these signs all manifest the proper conduct of government; whether the planets gather in Fang or in Jing, they ultimately attest the rise of a realm. For the encompassing heavens embody yang, and nothing escapes their illuminating scrutiny; when the armillary instrument measures the planets, their responses to things of like kind admit no deviation. Brilliantly these signs shine in the bamboo annals; distinctly they appear among the stars, the white elms of heaven.
Consider now Hanyu, displaying its auspicious orb. White as jade and yellow as gold, it ranks above Geze; in size it resembles a pellet, and its rays resemble a comet’s, signifying the sweeping away of Chanqiang, the baleful stars. It shone briefly in the Song era and was acclaimed as a marvel, but awaited the enlightened Ming age to manifest good government. This is surely because we reverently enjoy the reign of Your Majesty the Emperor…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
斗樞毓粹
日角昂姿
明晉德以自昭惟貞百度
察賁文而觀化時撫五辰
帝道大光
天工丕亮能誠則形形則著九功敘以興歌不
息則久久則徵七政齊而循軌茲者歲次
掩茂辰會玄枵瑞輝忽傍乎九游望舒逾
映殊彩更張於八彀津界爲蒙融灝灝之
===
元晶麗蒼蒼之正色拱乎
乾紐陸離呈十夕之祥助彼泰階璀璨增六符
之焰緣
聖化叶由庚之詠肆
天文快宣夜之稽喙息跂行普樂春臺壽域雕
題卉服各安桂海氷天匪今斯今已治益
治保章騰奏岳呼允愜乎輿情馮相告祺
時敕彌崇乎
聖志欽

punctuated: 斗樞毓粹，日角昂姿。明晉德以自昭，惟貞百度；察賁文而觀化，時撫五辰。帝道大光，天工丕亮。能誠則形，形則著，九功敘以興歌；不息則久，久則徵，七政齊而循軌。茲者歲次掩茂，辰會玄枵，瑞輝忽傍乎九游，望舒逾映；殊彩更張於八彀，津界爲蒙融。灝灝之元晶，麗蒼蒼之正色，拱乎乾紐，陸離呈十夕之祥；助彼泰階，璀璨增六符之焰。緣聖化叶由庚之詠，肆天文快宣夜之稽。喙息跂行，普樂春臺壽域；雕題卉服，各安桂海氷天。匪今斯今，已治益治。保章騰奏，岳呼允愜乎輿情；馮相告祺，時敕彌崇乎聖志。欽
translation_en:
…nurtured in the pure essence of the Dipper’s pivot, with the exalted bearing of a sun-like brow. You illuminate your advancing virtue and thereby make yourself illustrious, holding the hundred institutions to their proper course; you examine the patterned adornment of things and discern their transformation, duly governing the five celestial indicators. The imperial Way shines greatly; Heaven’s work is magnificently assisted. Perfect sincerity takes form, and what takes form becomes manifest: the nine achievements are ordered, inspiring songs of praise. Unceasing activity endures, and what endures produces evidence: the seven celestial luminaries are aligned and follow their courses.

Now, in the year designated Yanmao, with the celestial conjunction in Xuanxiao, auspicious radiance has suddenly appeared beside the Nine Streams constellation, outshining even Wangshu, the moon’s charioteer. Extraordinary colors spread anew across the eight expanses [?], and the bounds of the celestial ford grew hazy. The vast primordial brilliance, set against the true azure of heaven, attended the celestial pivot, displaying in shimmering splendor an auspicious sign for ten nights. It assisted the Three Steps constellation, adding a brilliant blaze to its six stars. Because your sage transforming influence accords with the ode You Geng, celestial patterns now gratifyingly bear out investigation according to the Xuanye account of heaven [?].

All creatures that breathe and move rejoice throughout a realm like a terrace of spring and a domain of longevity. Peoples with tattooed foreheads and garments of grass dwell at ease, from the cassia seas to the frozen skies. Never before has there been a present like this present: already well governed, the realm grows better governed still. The Astrologer hastens to submit his report; acclamations like those at Mount Song truly accord with the people’s feelings. The Astronomer announces auspicious signs; constant vigilance rises ever higher in Your Majesty’s sage resolve. Reverently …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
昊穹之簡眷戴
宗祏之明靈
閶闔頒
綸歸茂功而不宰典謨引
訓勉篤棐以加勤此其
聖不自聖之心所以優入於
聖域而
新又日新之德尤宜輻輳乎新禧者也臣士竒
景賢慚聚穎之荀遇
===
主愧起巖之傅叨聯四輔曳星履于
微垣忝切三台列
殿班于
華盖有爛之祥廛創見興視夜而雀躍奚勝無
前之懿爍忻逢
世如春而鴻聲合播爰模三頌美盛德之形
容敢綴四言鋪休徵之舄奕無闡
奎章而載筆瀆徼
電覽以為榮若被濩韶當聞樂而知德以登

黴垣忝切三台列
殿班于
華蓋有爛之祥矚創見興視夜而雀躍奚勝無
前之懿爍忻逢
世如春而鴻聲合擀羨模三頌美盛德之形
容敬綴四言鋪休徵之昜奭無闡
奎章而載筆瀆徽
睿覽以爲榮若被韺韶當聞樂而知德以登
punctuated:
昊穹之簡眷，戴宗祏之明靈。閶闔頒綸，歸茂功而不宰；典謨引訓，勉篤棐以加勤。此其聖不自聖之心，所以優入於聖域，而新又日新之德，尤宜輻輳乎新禧者也。
臣士竒、景賢，慚聚穎之荀，遇主愧起巖之傅。叨聯四輔，曳星履于微垣；忝切三台，列殿班于華盖。有爛之祥，廛創見，興視夜而雀躍奚勝；無前之懿，爍忻逢，世如春而鴻聲合播。爰模三頌，美盛德之形容；敢綴四言，鋪休徵之舄奕。無闡奎章而載筆，瀆徼電覽以為榮。若被濩韶，當聞樂而知德，以登
translation_en:
…Heaven’s discerning favor, and reverently uphold the radiant spirits of the ancestral shrines. From the palace gates an imperial pronouncement issues, attributing glorious achievements without claiming mastery over them; instruction is drawn from the ancient canons and counsels, urging devoted assistance and still greater diligence. Such is the mind of a sage who does not regard himself as a sage: through it, Your Majesty enters with ease into the realm of sagehood. Your virtue, renewed and renewed again each day, especially deserves the convergence of fresh blessings.
Your servants Shiqi and Jingxian feel unworthy beside Xun, whose outstanding sons gathered about him [?]; in encountering our sovereign, we feel ashamed beside Fu, raised from the cliffs. Undeservingly ranked among the Four Assistants, we trail our starry shoes within the celestial enclosure [?]; unworthily close to the Three Terraces, we take our places in the court ranks beneath the Imperial Canopy. These brilliant auspices are newly witnessed [the preceding 廛 is doubtful]; rising to observe the night, how could we contain our joy, leaping like sparrows? We rejoice to encounter this unprecedented, shining excellence [?]; the age is like spring, and voices of grand praise join in proclaiming it. Accordingly, we take the Three Eulogies as our models to praise the manifestations of abundant virtue. We venture to compose four-character verses, setting forth the splendor of these auspicious signs. Taking up our brushes to expound the imperial composition [?], we presumptuously seek the honor of Your Majesty’s lightning-bright perusal. As though graced by the music of Huo and Shao, one should hear the music and thereby know the virtue, so as to enter …

translation_en:
…the historical records, where words of praise will surely endure for all ages. The verses I offer are few; these words transmit a faithful account.
I humbly wish that the Northern Pole may pour down blessings and the Southern Pole prolong Your Majesty’s years; that the celestial axe of Jing may be laid away and the banner of Shen lowered, while jade-like radiance shines in the celestial treasury; that the winds governed by Ji and the rains governed by Bi may be duly regulated, and the harmonious light of the seasons shine through the celestial mechanism. Your servant, gazing toward Heaven and looking up in reverence to Your Sageliness, cannot contain his utmost joy and exultation. I respectfully submit the “Poem Congratulating Your Majesty on the Auspicious Star” that I have composed, accompanying this memorial, for Your Majesty’s attention.

His Majesty reverently cultivates virtue and thereby reaches Heaven, which sends down auspicious signs and grants its protection. His servants and people rejoice and sing praises, yet none perceives the essential meaning. This composition alone discerns the underlying source…

頌賛盛美，有得聖心之精，可以鳴聖治而垂無窮。佳士！佳士！

同考試官都給事中王批：皇上以至德隆膺天眷，天下臣民咸沐其休光，而莫能闡揚其盛。此作獨頌述精詳，而文采爛然，非有得於久道之化者不能也。敬服！敬服！

同考試官修撰諸批：我皇上純敬孚格上天，丕迓竒祥，光昭至治，真與帝堯合德，巍巍蕩蕩，如天難名。□此作乃能揄揚精悉，宜錄之以彰盛美於無窮云。

同考試官侍讀姜批：我皇上欽天之誠，承
translation_en:
…in praising His Majesty’s magnificent virtues and achievements, [the writer] has grasped the essence of the imperial mind. His words can proclaim the sage governance and transmit it for all time. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Chief Supervising Secretary: Through his consummate virtue, His Majesty has abundantly received Heaven’s favor. All officials and people throughout the realm bask in his gracious radiance, yet none has been able to elucidate and proclaim its magnificence. This composition alone offers praise and exposition both penetrating and detailed, with a brilliant literary style. Only someone who has gained understanding through the transforming influence of the Way long sustained could achieve this. I admire it with respect! I admire it with respect!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Senior Compiler: Our emperor’s pure reverence has moved Heaven through his sincerity. He has grandly welcomed extraordinary auspicious signs and splendidly manifested consummate governance. Truly, his virtue matches that of Emperor Yao: lofty and vast, like Heaven, it is difficult to describe. [Illegible character: □] This composition succeeds in celebrating it with precision and thoroughness. It should be recorded to make these magnificent virtues and achievements manifest for all time.

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
天之眷與唐堯同其盛美諸士類能鋪揚之矣至于莊誦

天記能析其精義條答問目則非尋常所可及此必涵育

曰欽者聖學之要至讀堯典見堯德之首於欽
也亦未嘗不起羮墻之思爾今躬逢

punctuated:
天之眷，與唐堯同其盛美，諸士類能鋪揚之矣。至于莊誦御製《欽天記》，能析其精義，條答問目，則非尋常所可及。此必涵育聖化之深而有得者乎！
考試官學士嚴批：夫學者稽古論譔，孰不曰「欽者聖學之要」？至讀《堯典》，見堯德之首於欽也，亦未嘗不起羮墻之思。爾今躬逢聖人，又得仰誦聖製，仰窺聖學，而聖化之盛，因仰贊焉，爾真如在堯世矣！篇內鋪揚皇天眷命，類如益之贊堯。爾其益勉為堯臣哉！
考試官學士李批：皇上欽承天眷，製為記頌，即古帝堯欽天之心莫加也。子能敬揚其盛，其亦涵育聖化而有得者乎！
translation_en:
…Heaven’s favor, matching Tang Yao in this splendid excellence: the candidates have generally been able to expound and celebrate it. But reverently reading the imperially composed Account of Revering Heaven (Qin tian ji), analyzing its essential meaning, and answering the questions point by point—this lies beyond ordinary ability. Surely this writer has been deeply nurtured by the sage’s transforming influence and gained understanding from it!
Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: Among scholars who investigate antiquity and compose discussions, who does not say, “Reverence is the essential principle of sagely learning”? When they read the Canon of Yao and see that reverence stands foremost among Yao’s virtues, they invariably feel a longing for him, as though seeing him in their broth or upon the wall. You now live in the presence of a sage; moreover, you can reverently recite his writings, glimpse his sagely learning, and thereby praise the flourishing of his transforming influence. You truly seem to be living in Yao’s age! Your essay’s exposition and celebration of August Heaven’s favor and mandate resembles Yi’s praise of Yao. Strive still harder to become a minister worthy of Yao!
Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: His Majesty reverently receives Heaven’s favor and has composed an account and a eulogy. Even the ancient Emperor Yao’s reverence for Heaven could not surpass his. You have been able respectfully to celebrate this excellence. Surely you too have been nurtured by the sage’s transforming influence and gained understanding from it!

translation_en: Heaven bestows supreme auspicious signs; the sage receives them, and his Way shines forth. The sage reverently serves Heaven; Heaven all the more faithfully protects him, and his blessed reign flourishes. Brightly manifest below and radiantly resplendent above—this is the working by which they become one. Heaven has no favorites; it favors those capable of reverence. This is the natural principle. Thus, great indeed are the sage’s words! Through them the sage fittingly receives Heaven’s favor. Undivided indeed is the sage’s heart! Through it Heaven increasingly magnifies its favor toward the sage. In the dealings between Heaven and the sage, there truly is a full and trusting mutual accord [?]. As for the sage’s reverence for Heaven, how fully and splendidly it has been recorded since antiquity! translation_en:
…shares the same virtue as Your Majesty; in reverently following August Heaven, he shares the same Way as Your Majesty; and in receiving sweet dew, he shares the same auspicious sign as Your Majesty. Thus you, honored examiners, have praised them together, and I, your humble student, venture accordingly to extol them both with reverence.
I have heard that in the ninth year of Jiajing [1530], on the day welcoming the lengthening of daylight, when yang first arose, Your Majesty reverently performed the great rite of thanksgiving at the Circular Mound. That very evening, pearl-like drizzle spread auspicious blessings, and blue-gray mist gathered into an auspicious sign. Not long afterward, Heaven sent sweet dew down upon the sepulchral chamber of Your Majesty’s deceased father. Its guardians reported this, and Your Majesty received it reverently. In the following year, on an auspicious jia day in the second month of spring, Your Majesty again visited the Circular Mound to give thanks for the Supreme Deity’s gift. You thereupon composed the Record and Ode on Revering Heaven, bestowed it upon the meritorious nobles, grand secretaries, court lecturers, and other ministers, and disseminated it throughout the realm. Thus I, your humble student, have been able reverently to apprehend its general import.
Dew is the moisture of harmonious vital energies; when sweet, it is the essence of Xuanyuan [the Yellow Emperor], the liquid of Heaven’s milk. As the Illustrations of Auspicious Signs puts it, “Auspicious signs that emerge…”

translation_en:
…from Heaven, and ranks highest among auspicious signs. Now, when this sweet dew fell, its timing coincided precisely with the suburban sacrifice to Heaven, and its location was the resting place of the spirit of His Majesty’s deceased father. This was indeed an especially auspicious sign. Formerly, during the lifetime of His Majesty’s deceased father, sweet dew once fell at night and gathered upon the branches. He tasted it and thereupon composed a poem on sweet dew, already declaring it a portent of blessings. His Majesty did indeed answer the flourishing destiny that comes once in five hundred years: lightning encircled and a rainbow streamed—portents of his birth—thus inaugurating boundless blessings for our dynasty for countless ages. Heaven’s favor had long been fixed upon him, and auspicious portents appeared beforehand. How could these be signs that have appeared only now?

I have humbly heard that when His Majesty’s deceased father instructed the ministers undertaking ritual purification, he admonished them to carry out their duties with focused and undivided attention. When addressing the ministers who assisted and guided him, he spoke of his own vigilance, reverence, and awe. The court lecturers accordingly praised the meticulousness of his moral cultivation and the depth of his attainment. Through utmost sincerity, one can know things beforehand. His Majesty’s deceased father possessed utmost sincerity; how could he not have known beforehand?

I have reverently consulted the various books on auspicious responses. They say: “When sagely virtue reaches upward to the Great Purity of Heaven and downward to the myriad spirits, sweet dew falls.” They also say: “When a king’s virtue reaches Heaven and harmonious vital energy flourishes, sweet dew falls.” Again: “When the ruler’s government brings perfect peace, sweet dew falls.” Again: “When the elderly receive respect, sweet dew falls.” Again: “When benevolence extends to all things, sweet dew falls.” Viewed in light of the present…

translation_en: …precisely describes our Emperor. Thus, its falling in former times heralded the sage; its falling now responds to the sage. Heaven’s intent is exceedingly clear. Yet our Emperor does not claim sagehood for himself, but only reveres Heaven. Reverently reciting his imperial composition, grand and august, we find nothing in it that does not express reverence. Such phrases as “From above I receive the favor of being chosen,” “From above I receive exceptional regard,” “The dew descends as a supreme auspice,” “Precious dew brings down blessings,” “I bow my head in wonder,” and “How could my gratitude for this grace ever cease?” express his sincerity in treasuring and cherishing it. Such words as “Thus I consult the counsels of the many, looking to offer recompense at the Circular Mound; truly fearful, truly apprehensive, I dread only that my efforts may fall short” express the ritual propriety of requiting this favor. Such words as “My imperial ancestor’s divine achievements surpass the present and excel antiquity, bequeathing to me, his humble descendant, the blessings received from Heaven,” and “My imperial father’s mysterious virtue—he ascended unseen…”

text:

天之保是稱

punctuated: 穹昊，延予小子荷天之保。」是稱親之孝也。若曰「祗竭愚衷」，若曰「嘉貺眇昧」，是撝謙之光也。若曰「兆民其綏」，若曰「福我下民」，是子民之仁也。若曰「敢甘自侈，夙夜勉修」，若曰「朝夕惕然，上稟眷命」，是保祚之慎也。夫若此者，皆聖心之欽爲之也。欽存於心，是謂先天而天弗違，天之所以眷也，是所由致瑞者也。欽形於言，是謂後天而奉天時，天之所以益眷也，是所由益致瑞者也。是故瑞見於天，則爲景星、爲慶雲；瑞見於地，則爲河清、爲醴泉；瑞見於品彙，則爲嘉禾、爲瑞麥、爲秀芝、爲雙瓜、爲素鵲、爲玄鶴、爲白鹿、爲黃兎、爲麒麟。其他斗極明，日月光，壽曜熈，泰階平，時暘而暘，時雨而雨，自如甘露之外，應圖合牒，卓犖踵臻，
translation_en:
… the vast heavens, extending blessings to me, his young descendant, so that I receive Heaven’s protection.” This is the filial devotion that extols one’s parent. Such words as “Reverently I exhaust my humble sincerity” and “These gracious gifts [come to one who is] insignificant and unenlightened [?]” display the radiance of humility. Such words as “May the myriad people be at peace” and “Bless my common people” express the benevolence of treating the people as one’s children. Such words as “Would I dare indulge in extravagance? Day and night I strive to cultivate myself” and “Morning and evening I remain vigilant, reverently receiving Heaven’s gracious mandate” express the care taken to preserve the imperial succession. All these arise from reverence within the sagely heart. When reverence abides in the heart, this is what is meant by “preceding Heaven, yet Heaven does not oppose him.” This is why Heaven bestows its favor, and how auspicious signs are brought forth. When reverence takes shape in words, this is what is meant by “following Heaven and observing Heaven’s seasons.” This is why Heaven bestows still greater favor, and how still more auspicious signs are brought forth.

Thus, when auspicious signs appear in Heaven, they take the form of felicitous stars and auspicious clouds; when they appear on earth, they take the form of the Yellow River running clear and springs of sweet water; when they appear among living things, they take the form of auspicious grain, auspicious wheat, flourishing numinous mushrooms, twin melons, white magpies, black cranes, white deer, yellow hares, and qilin. There are also the brightness of the Dipper and the Pole Star, the brilliance of the sun and moon, the radiance of the Star of Longevity, and the balanced disposition of the Three Steps stars; sunshine comes when sunshine is due, and rain when rain is due. Besides such things as sweet dew [?], extraordinary signs corresponding to the prophetic charts and tallying with the records arrive one after another …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
豈可勝道哉而要之則皆
皇上之欽之所致也盖
皇上欽存於心無所不篤欽形於言無所不踐
是故
感雨輒吟喜雪輒謌
靈貺絡繹
宸翰炳蔚是無所不珍佩也
爲國爲民
躬厥禱請靡
===
神不舉靡典不秩祈之孔夙應之孔神而報賽
不暮是無所不申禀也遡
太祖之肇始念
成祖之緝成追
皇考之慶延配
天配
帝
祖報
宗稱

translation_en:
…how could they all be recounted? In sum, they are all brought about by His Majesty’s reverence. For His Majesty harbors reverence in his heart, remaining earnest in every respect; he expresses reverence in his words, putting every one into practice. Thus, moved by rain, he invariably composes verse; rejoicing in snow, he invariably sings. Divine blessings arrive in unbroken succession, and his imperial writings shine resplendently: there is nothing he does not cherish and hold reverently.

For the dynasty and the people, he personally offers prayers and petitions. No spirit is left without an offering, and no rite is left without its proper ordering. His prayers are offered most promptly, their responses are most wondrous, and his thanksgiving offerings are never late: there is nothing concerning which he fails to submit his petitions reverently. He looks back to Taizu’s founding achievement, reflects upon Chengzu’s work of consolidating it, and recalls the blessings extending from his deceased imperial father. He associates them in sacrifice with Heaven and with the Supreme Deity, offers recompense to his progenitors, and extols his ancestors…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
玄功盛德謂同
高厚是無所不稱
親也不自謂眇則自謂冲是無所不撝謙也
郊祀樂章則願生民蒙福
祈穀祝文則願萬方咸頼胞視之軫念之懷
保之於是乎為之勸農為之蠲租為之賑
饑為之療疫為之拯墊為之矜寃是無所
不子民也
亹亹翼翼惟時惟幾一霾示儆修省惟惕一
===
隅告祲驅除惟駛近之
宫庭遠之綏荒細之幾微大之綱紀内之臺
省外之岳牧燭之若曦暉運之若風霆毖
之若竍蜂戒之若衣袽持之若金甌是無
所不保祚也夫若此者皆欽也皆善事乎
天之實也是故典則惇厥天叙矣禮則庸厥天
秩矣德則章厥天命矣罪則刑厥天討矣
化四達教四訖澤四被海晏徼謐民康物阜
而天下益太平矣

punctuated:
玄功盛德，謂同高厚，是無所不稱親也。不自謂眇，則自謂冲，是無所不撝謙也。郊祀樂章則願生民蒙福，祈穀祝文則願萬方咸頼。胞視之，軫念之，懷保之，於是乎為之勸農，為之蠲租，為之賑饑，為之療疫，為之拯墊，為之矜寃，是無所不子民也。
亹亹翼翼，惟時惟幾。一霾示儆，修省惟惕；一隅告祲，驅除惟駛。近之宫庭，遠之綏荒，細之幾微，大之綱紀，内之臺省，外之岳牧，燭之若曦暉，運之若風霆，毖之若竍蜂，戒之若衣袽，持之若金甌，是無所不保祚也。
夫若此者，皆欽也，皆善事乎天之實也。是故典則惇厥天叙矣，禮則庸厥天秩矣，德則章厥天命矣，罪則刑厥天討矣。化四達，教四訖，澤四被，海晏徼謐，民康物阜，而天下益太平矣。
translation_en:
…their mysterious achievements and abundant virtue are declared equal to lofty Heaven and the broad Earth: in every respect he extols his forebears. If he does not call himself insignificant, he calls himself immature: in every respect he practices humility. In the musical hymns for the suburban sacrifices, he wishes that the people may receive blessings; in the prayer for grain, he wishes that all regions may benefit. He regards the people as his siblings, thinks solicitously of them, and cherishes and protects them. Thus he encourages agriculture for them, remits their taxes, relieves their hunger, treats their epidemics, rescues them from floods, and shows compassion for those wronged. In every respect he treats the people as his children.
Diligent and reverent, he attends to the proper moment and the first stirrings of events. When a single haze gives warning, he fearfully examines and reforms himself; when one corner of the realm reports an ominous influence, he hastens to dispel it. Whether near at hand in the palace or far away in pacifying remote lands, whether in subtle beginnings or the great principles of government, whether among the central censorial and administrative offices or the regional governors, he illuminates affairs like sunlight and sets them in motion like wind and thunder. He exercises caution as against stinging insects [?], takes precautions as one keeps old cloth ready to plug a boat’s leaks, and safeguards the realm as though it were a golden bowl. In every respect he preserves the dynasty’s allotted fortune.
All such conduct is reverence; all is the substance of serving Heaven well. Thus, through the established norms he gives due weight to Heaven’s ordering of human relationships; through ritual he puts Heaven’s graded distinctions into practice; through rewarding virtue he makes Heaven’s mandate manifest; and through punishing offenses he executes Heaven’s chastisements. His transforming influence reaches in all four directions, his instruction extends to every limit, and his beneficence spreads everywhere. The seas are calm, the frontiers tranquil, the people secure, and resources abundant: all under Heaven enjoys ever greater peace.

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
天地訢合太和薫蒸而安得不致夫諸瑞哉夫
堯之欽若昊天也心之欽也惟欽故明惟
欽明故文思安安允恭克讓而克明乎峻
德惟峻德克明故廣運焉而大洽夫敦睦
辯章時雍迂衡之化是故其致瑞也亦匪
直甘露而已也翼軫之間景星見焉河渚
之間昴精飛焉河圖來焉醴泉溢焉蓂莢
生焉神禾敷焉鳳巢阿閣焉龍遊宫沼焉
神龜自越裳獻焉而天之眷堯者隆矣由
===
此觀之聖人感之而天應之天感之而聖
人應之聖人又感之而天又應之蓋天與
聖人交相感應而堯與
皇上實相後先是故堯有煥然之文章
皇上亦有煥然之文章堯有巍然之成功
皇上亦有巍然之成功而本之則欽也在堯爲
精一在
皇上爲敬一而感應之所以神也先聖
後聖其揆一也此之謂也

punctuated: 天地訢合，太和薫蒸，而安得不致夫諸瑞哉？夫堯之欽若昊天也，心之欽也。惟欽故明，惟欽明故文思安安，允恭克讓，而克明乎峻德。惟峻德克明，故廣運焉，而大洽夫敦睦、辯章、時雍、迂衡之化。是故其致瑞也，亦匪直甘露而已也。翼軫之間，景星見焉；河渚之間，昴精飛焉；河圖來焉，醴泉溢焉，蓂莢生焉，神禾敷焉，鳳巢阿閣焉，龍遊宫沼焉，神龜自越裳獻焉，而天之眷堯者隆矣。由此觀之，聖人感之而天應之，天感之而聖人應之，聖人又感之而天又應之。蓋天與聖人交相感應，而堯與皇上實相後先。是故堯有煥然之文章，皇上亦有煥然之文章；堯有巍然之成功，皇上亦有巍然之成功。而本之則欽也。在堯爲精一，在皇上爲敬一，而感應之所以神也。「先聖後聖，其揆一也」，此之謂也。
translation_en:
Heaven and earth unite in harmony, and supreme concord pervades all: how could this fail to bring forth the many auspicious signs? Yao’s reverent conformity to August Heaven was reverence of the heart. Through reverence he attained illumination; through reverence and illumination, he was cultured and thoughtful, naturally at ease, truly respectful and capable of yielding, and able to manifest his lofty virtue. Because his lofty virtue was manifest, its influence extended far and wide, fully spreading the transforming effects of familial concord, the distinguishing and clarification of ranks, universal harmony, and “yu heng” [?]. Thus the auspicious signs he brought forth were by no means limited to sweet dew. Between the lunar lodges Yi and Zhen, an auspicious star appeared; among the river islets, the essence of the lunar lodge Mao flew forth. The River Chart arrived; sweet springs overflowed; the auspicious mingjia plant grew; divine grain flourished; phoenixes nested in the lofty pavilion; dragons swam in the palace pond; and a divine tortoise was presented from Yueshang. Heaven’s favor toward Yao was indeed abundant.

Viewed in this light, the sage moves Heaven, and Heaven responds; Heaven moves the sage, and the sage responds; the sage moves Heaven again, and Heaven again responds. Heaven and the sage thus move and respond to one another, and Yao and His Majesty truly follow one another in this succession. Thus Yao possessed resplendent cultural achievements, and His Majesty likewise possesses resplendent cultural achievements; Yao accomplished towering deeds, and His Majesty likewise has accomplished towering deeds. At their root lies reverence. In Yao this took the form of purity and singleness of mind; in His Majesty, reverence and singleness of mind. This is what makes their mutual influence and response with Heaven so wondrous. “The sages of earlier and later ages follow the same measure”: this is what those words mean.

text:
第二問
張烈
同考試官都給事中趙批我
皇上好生之德與虞舜欽恤之仁暨我
祖宗諭臣之意先後同符此作敷暢明悉盖涵濡而有得者
同考試官檢討馬批我
皇上矜察無辜之心遠稽堯舜近法
祖宗前後一揆子能紬繹問意而責慎於司牧是誠體要之論
同考試官檢討晁批我
===

皇上好生之心同符堯舜子能歷歷揄揚之可以風天下矣
同考試官編修曹批我
皇上好生之仁子能一一闡悉使天下曉然仰體
至意刑措之隆庶亦有助焉宜錄之
考試官學士嚴批此作能仰體我
皇上好生大德仁民至意而詳發之必亦志於仁者
考試官學士李批策人能志用刑本意而於我

punctuated:
第二問
張烈

同考試官都給事中趙批：「我皇上好生之德，與虞舜欽恤之仁，暨我祖宗諭臣之意，先後同符。此作敷暢明悉，盖涵濡而有得者。」

同考試官檢討馬批：「我皇上矜察無辜之心，遠稽堯舜，近法祖宗，前後一揆。子能紬繹問意，而責慎於司牧，是誠體要之論。」

同考試官檢討晁批：「我穆宗暨我皇上好生之心，同符堯舜。子能歷歷揄揚之，可以風天下矣。」

同考試官編修曹批：「我皇上好生之仁，子能一一闡悉，使天下曉然仰體至意，刑措之隆，庶亦有助焉，宜錄之。」

考試官學士嚴批：「此作能仰體我皇上好生大德、仁民至意，而詳發之，必亦志於仁者。」

考試官學士李批：「策人能志用刑本意，而於我皇上好生之德，又能仰窺而揄揚之，出必不負于時者。佳士！佳士！」
translation_en:
Second Question
Zhang Lie

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Our Emperor’s virtue of cherishing life accords with the benevolence of Shun of Yu in exercising reverent care and compassion in punishment, and with the intentions expressed by our imperial ancestors in their instructions to their ministers. Across the ages, these are in accord. This essay expounds these matters fluently, clearly, and fully; its author has evidently absorbed these teachings and gained understanding.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Examining Editor: “Our Emperor’s compassionate concern to scrutinize the cases of the innocent looks back to Yao and Shun as distant precedents and follows our imperial ancestors as nearer models: the guiding principle is the same throughout. You can draw out the meaning of the question and demand caution from those who shepherd the people. This is indeed a discussion that grasps the essentials.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor: “The hearts of our Muzong [?] and our Emperor, cherishing life, accord with those of Yao and Shun. You can set forth and extol this point by point, thereby providing moral instruction to all under Heaven.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cao, Compiler: “You can elucidate, point by point and in full, our Emperor’s benevolence in cherishing life, enabling all under Heaven clearly to comprehend and reverently embody his deepest intentions. This may also contribute to the flourishing state in which punishments are laid aside. It merits selection.”

Comment by Examiner Yan, Academician: “This essay can reverently comprehend our Emperor’s great virtue of cherishing life and his deepest intention to treat the people benevolently, and expound them in detail. Its author must also be someone whose aspirations are set upon benevolence.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician: “The writer of this policy essay can keep in mind the original purpose of employing punishments. He can also reverently discern and extol our Emperor’s virtue of cherishing life. On entering public service, he will surely not fail the needs of his time. A worthy scholar! A worthy scholar!”

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
嘗謂民者天之所生天之所生則天欲生
之而苟不得其生則天矜之故好生者天
之心也仁也天之大德也而人君者則天
以斯民托之使生者也天以托君君則以
托臣無非以生斯民也君能體天所托乎
民之心而心乎好生則臣當體君所托乎
民之心而亦心乎好生夫苟心乎好生則
無所不用其仁即不得已而至於刑民亦
以生之之心用之而以生之之道行之惟
===
以戢其相戕乎生者而使之相生即刑之
者苟不至乎相戕之甚則亦仁之而使之
並生是故有弗刑刑之無弗當有弗罰罰
之無弗中是爲能體君之心臣體君之心
則君亦賴以體天之心是故刑罰清而民
服民服則有以感其心而和平將日遷善
遠罪而相安其生故曰惟天好生惟聖時
憲惟臣欽若惟民從乂不然則民有不得
其生者矣嗚呼民則易虐矣其如君心何

punctuated: 嘗謂民者天之所生，天之所生則天欲生之，而苟不得其生則天矜之。故好生者天之心也，仁也，天之大德也。而人君者，則天以斯民托之使生者也。天以托君，君則以托臣，無非以生斯民也。君能體天所托乎民之心而心乎好生，則臣當體君所托乎民之心而亦心乎好生。夫苟心乎好生，則無所不用其仁。即不得已而至於刑民，亦以生之之心用之，而以生之之道行之，惟以戢其相戕乎生者而使之相生。即刑之者，苟不至乎相戕之甚，則亦仁之而使之並生。是故有弗刑，刑之無弗當；有弗罰，罰之無弗中。是爲能體君之心。臣體君之心，則君亦賴以體天之心。是故刑罰清而民服，民服則有以感其心而和平，將日遷善遠罪而相安其生。故曰：「惟天好生，惟聖時憲，惟臣欽若，惟民從乂。」不然，則民有不得其生者矣。嗚呼！民則易虐矣，其如君心何
translation_en: I have often said that the people are born of Heaven. Since Heaven gives them birth, Heaven desires that they live; if they cannot secure their lives, Heaven pities them. Thus cherishing life is Heaven’s heart: it is benevolence, Heaven’s great virtue. The ruler is the one to whom Heaven entrusts these people so that they may live. Heaven entrusts them to the ruler, and the ruler entrusts them to his ministers—all for the sake of sustaining these people. If the ruler can embody Heaven’s concern in entrusting the people to him and set his heart on cherishing life, then his ministers should embody the ruler’s concern in entrusting the people to them and likewise set their hearts on cherishing life. If they truly cherish life, they will exercise benevolence in everything. Even when compelled to punish the people, they will apply punishment with the intention of preserving life and carry it out in ways that preserve life, solely to restrain people from destroying one another’s lives and enable them to sustain one another. Even those whom they punish, provided their destruction of others’ lives has not reached an extreme, should also be treated benevolently and allowed to live alongside others. Thus some are left unpunished, but whenever punishment is imposed, it is invariably appropriate; some are spared penalties, but whenever penalties are imposed, they invariably fit the offense. This is what it means to embody the ruler’s heart. When ministers embody the ruler’s heart, the ruler in turn relies on them to embody Heaven’s heart. Thus punishments are administered fairly and the people submit. Their submission makes it possible to move their hearts toward harmony and peace; day by day they will advance toward goodness, distance themselves from wrongdoing, and live together in security. Hence it is said: “Heaven cherishes life; the sage takes this as his model; ministers reverently comply; the people follow and are well governed.” Otherwise, some among the people will be unable to secure their lives. Alas! The people may be easy to oppress, but how could one answer to the ruler’s heart…

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
哉其如天心何哉愚盖因仰睹
皇上有
勅訓司牧者而有慨焉
勅中稱古昔帝王及我
祖宗罔不慎重於刑夫古昔帝王之心好生之
心也夫我
祖宗之心好生之心也夫我
皇上之心好生之心也是好生之心也天之心
也有是好生之心如天則不容不慎重於
===
刑是故
皇上之心與我
祖宗之心與古昔帝王之心一也是故
勅中稱之也夫古昔帝王慎重之訓布在方冊
往往而是欲悉數之乃留更僕未易數也
是故執事不質愚以所共曉者但質其擬
議焉而有深意存者然而方冊所布亦無

…! And how could they answer to Heaven’s heart? I have been moved to reflection by reverently reading His Majesty’s edict instructing those who shepherd the people. The edict states that the sovereigns of antiquity and our imperial ancestors invariably exercised care in punishment. The heart of the ancient sovereigns was a heart that cherished life; the heart of our imperial ancestors was a heart that cherished life; and the heart of His Majesty is a heart that cherishes life. This heart that cherishes life is Heaven’s heart. Possessing such a heart, which cherishes life as Heaven does, one cannot fail to exercise care in punishment. Thus His Majesty’s heart, the heart of our imperial ancestors, and the heart of the ancient sovereigns are one. That is why the edict speaks of them.
The ancient sovereigns’ teachings on exercising care are recorded throughout the books. Were one to enumerate them all, even lingering through changes of attendants [?], one could not readily finish the count. Hence you, honored examiners, do not question me about what everyone understands, but only about matters requiring deliberation and containing profound meaning. Nevertheless, what is recorded in the books is all encompassed here. In the Book of Changes, five hexagrams speak of administering punishments and judicial proceedings: Shihe (Biting Through), Feng (Abundance), Bi (Adornment), Lü (The Traveler), and Zhongfu (Inner Sincerity). title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
也震也艮也獨取於象者二巽也兌也析
而言之其義各殊統而言之則皆慎重乎
刑而已噬嗑之象則曰明罰勅法賁則曰
明庶政無敢折獄旅則曰明慎用刑而不
留獄豐則曰折獄致刑中孚則曰議獄緩
死夫曰明曰勅曰慎曰折曰議曰緩曰不
留曰無敢折聖人之訓至章章也卦所取
象有離有震有艮震為雷離為電為火艮
為山震固取其威矣離取其光而照之必
===
明艮取其靜而止之不過是故噬嗑與豐
取雷取電賁與旅取山取火而四卦或上
或下皆有離焉或取電或取火其取於光
明之義均也故明者尤治刑獄之要道也
聖人之意可知也故書曰明允曰明啟曰
明清傳曰明徵曰察必以情皆是道也至
於中孚雖取兌巽而其全體似離互體則
有震艮聖人惓惓焉寓意之深也夫既明
以照之無隱情矣然後威之夫既威之則

translation_en:
… Zhen, and Gen. Two are drawn upon individually for their images: Xun and Dui. Considered separately, their meanings differ; considered together, they all amount to caution and care in punishment. The Image Commentary for Shihe (Biting Through) says: “Clarify punishments and put the laws in order.” For Bi (Adornment), it says: “Clarify the various affairs of government, but do not venture to adjudicate lawsuits.” For Lü (The Wanderer), it says: “Be discerning and cautious in applying punishments, and do not let lawsuits linger.” For Feng (Abundance), it says: “Adjudicate lawsuits and carry out punishments.” For Zhongfu (Inner Sincerity), it says: “Deliberate upon criminal cases and defer executions.” These injunctions—to be discerning, to put in order, to exercise caution, to adjudicate, to deliberate, to defer, not to let cases linger, and not to venture to adjudicate—make the sages’ teaching abundantly clear.

The trigrams from which these hexagrams draw their images include Li, Zhen, and Gen. Zhen represents thunder; Li, lightning and fire; and Gen, a mountain. Zhen is indeed invoked for its awe-inspiring power; Li is invoked for its light, so that illumination must be clear; Gen is invoked for its stillness, so that restraint prevents excess. Thus Shihe and Feng draw upon thunder and lightning, while Bi and Lü draw upon mountain and fire. All four hexagrams contain Li, either above or below. Whether they draw upon lightning or fire, they share equally in the meaning of illumination. Discernment is therefore an especially essential principle in handling criminal cases. From this we can understand the sages’ intention. Thus the Book of Documents speaks of “discernment and fairness,” “clearly disclosing,” and “clear scrutiny”; the Commentary speaks of “clear verification” and says, “In examining cases, one must ascertain the actual circumstances.” All express this same principle.

As for Zhongfu, although it draws upon Dui and Xun, its overall configuration resembles Li, while its nuclear trigrams include Zhen and Gen. How profound is the meaning that the sages, in their earnest solicitude, lodged within it! Once matters have been illuminated with discernment, no circumstances remain concealed; only then is awe-inspiring authority brought to bear. Once that authority has been brought to bear, then …

title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
遂止之及獄之既成又兌以議之巽以緩
之陳之以時臯即之以天論王聽之司寇
聽之三公聽之旬而職聽三旬而職聽三
月而上之議而又議緩而又緩求其出不
可得然後入之求其生不可得然後死之
是中孚所取於兌巽之義也夫兌為澤而
巽為風水體虛風動之人心虛物感之是
故有所議有所緩本諸至誠惻怛之心而
行其不殺不辜之仁是中孚所取於兌巽
===
之義也且風無形而能動乎澤誠無象而
能動乎人是故舜德好生舜之中孚也民
不犯於有司天下之中孚也而上下相孚
如風澤之交矣是中孚所取於兌巽之義
也聖人之意可知也夫聖人之意寓於易
而聖人之政則具於書虞書曰欽哉欽哉
惟刑之恤哉此正舜好生之德也而惟臯
陶知之故賛舜曰御眾以寬曰罪疑惟輕
夫臯陶能知舜是亦有舜好生之心故舜

遂止之。及獄之既成，又兌以議之，巽以緩之，陳之以時臯，即之以天論。王聽之，司寇聽之，三公聽之；旬而職聽，三旬而職聽，三月而上之。議而又議，緩而又緩，求其出不可得，然後入之；求其生不可得，然後死之。是中孚所取於兌巽之義也。夫兌為澤，而巽為風，水體虛，風動之；人心虛，物感之。是故有所議，有所緩，本諸至誠惻怛之心，而行其不殺不辜之仁，是中孚所取於兌巽之義也。且風無形而能動乎澤，誠無象而能動乎人。是故舜德好生，舜之中孚也；民不犯於有司，天下之中孚也。而上下相孚，如風澤之交矣，是中孚所取於兌巽之義也。聖人之意可知也。

…then brings them to a stop. Once the judicial case has been established, one further employs the yielding joy of Dui to deliberate upon it and the gentleness of Xun to defer its execution. One sets it forth according to “shi gao” [?] and brings it into accord with Heaven’s judgments [?]. The king hears it; the Minister of Justice hears it; the Three Dukes hear it. After ten days it receives an official hearing [?], and after thirty days another official hearing [?]; after three months it is submitted to the throne. Deliberation follows deliberation, and delay follows delay. Only when no way can be found to acquit the accused is he convicted; only when no way can be found to preserve his life is he put to death. This is the meaning that the hexagram Zhongfu (Inner Sincerity) draws from Dui and Xun. Dui represents a lake, and Xun represents wind. Water is receptive in its substance, and wind moves it; the human heart is receptive, and things affect it. Thus deliberation and delay are rooted in a heart of utmost sincerity and compassion, putting into practice the benevolence that refuses to kill the innocent. This is the meaning that Zhongfu draws from Dui and Xun. Moreover, wind has no form, yet can move the lake; sincerity has no visible appearance, yet can move people. Thus Shun’s virtue of cherishing life was Shun’s inner sincerity; the people’s committing no offenses before the responsible authorities was the inner sincerity of all under Heaven. Those above and below responded to one another in trust, like the interaction of wind and lake. This is the meaning that Zhongfu draws from Dui and Xun. The sages’ intention can thus be understood.
The sages’ intention is lodged in the Book of Changes, while their principles of government are fully set out in the Book of Documents. The Documents of Yu says: “Be reverent! Be reverent! Be compassionate in matters of punishment!” This precisely expresses Shun’s virtue of cherishing life. Gao Yao alone understood it, and therefore, in praising Shun, said: “Govern the multitude with leniency,” and: “When guilt is doubtful, favor the lighter punishment.” That Gao Yao could understand Shun means that he too possessed Shun’s heart of cherishing life. title: 嘉靖三十八年會試錄
text:
知之乃命作士五服三就五宅三居其所
命之職也期于予治期于無刑其所命之
心也皐陶於是持其慎憲之心行其安民
之惠而成其風動從欲之治故舜嘉之曰
惟乃休曰時乃功曰方祗厥敘而禹亦曰
皐陶德乃降黎民懷之故愚謂舜與皐陶
上下之志同也同於好生也是君臣相成
之準也其詳具虞書中夫人而知之矣甫
刑乃曰伯夷降典折民惟刑又曰伯夷播
===
刑之迪夫伯夷吾知舜命之作秩宗矣命
之典三禮矣初何與於刑者而甫刑顧此
云也夫孔子至聖眾言折衷孔子嘗曰禮
樂不興則刑罰不中又曰古之知法者能
省刑本也今之知法者不失有罪末矣是
故舜命伯夷教民以禮民入於禮而不入
於刑所以折絕斯民入刑之路務其本也
甫刑之論是探本之論也漢刑法志述之
亦謂制禮以止刑猶隄之防溢水也知甫
